Policy version log and archived prior versions
Annual review record and rule-change review notes
Employee acknowledgment signatures
Staff training sign-in sheets for policy changes
Review calendar

policies.title: Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency license limited to non-skilled services (all client records and all service lines); the same review method is applied to the Homemaker and Companion Services line, if offered, using the confidential client record (REC-02)
policies.purpose: To operate an ongoing quality assurance (QA) program that checks, at least every quarter, whether [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients it can serve, delivers services consistent with each client's service plan, documents them properly, follows its own policies and protects client confidentiality. The program also ensures that findings lead to documented improvements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains an ongoing QA program under Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(e), F.A.C. At least quarterly, a documented review is made of a sample of active and closed client records. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(e)1-7, F.A.C., as follows. Item 1: the review assures the agency accepts only clients whose service needs it can meet. Item 2: it assures case assignment and case management are appropriate, adequate and consistent with the service plan, and that service plans are individualized. Item 3: it assures that services provided by aides, CNAs, the RN supervisor and any other staff are coordinated, appropriate, adequate and consistent with the plan. Item 4: it assures that all services and outcomes are completely and legibly documented, dated and signed in the client record. Item 5: it assures the agency's policies and procedures are followed. Item 6: it assures the confidentiality of client data is maintained. Item 7: QA findings are used to improve services, and each corrective action is documented. The Administrator is accountable for the program and reports results to the Governing Body.

definitions.definition: The record of a client who is currently receiving services from the agency.
The record of a client who has been discharged, transferred or has otherwise ended services.
A calendar quarter (January-March, April-June, July-September, October-December). One documented review is completed in each quarter.
A specific, assigned and dated step taken to fix a deficiency found in QA review and to prevent its recurrence.
The Registered Nurse supervisor, the Administrator, or another qualified person designated in writing by the Administrator. A reviewer does not review his or her own work where practical.

procedures: By the first week of each calendar quarter, the Administrator designates in writing the QA reviewer(s) for the quarter and sets the review date. The review is completed before the end of the quarter.

The reviewer draws a sample of both active and closed client records. As the agency's standard, the sample is at least 10 percent of each group, and no fewer than 5 records of each group (or all records if fewer exist). The sample includes records of each caregiver type (CNA, home health aide, and homemaker/companion if applicable), each payer type, and any client discharged for a safety concern or complaint.

The reviewer records the sample selection method and the records reviewed on the QA Record Review Form ([FORM NAME]), identifying records by client ID rather than by name on any summary shared outside the QA team.

Item 1 (acceptance of clients): for each sampled record, the reviewer checks that the intake and assessment (SVC-03) show the client's needs fall within the agency's licensed non-skilled scope and staffing, and that any client whose needs exceeded the agency's capability was referred elsewhere instead of accepted.

Item 2 (case assignment and management): the reviewer checks that the caregiver assigned matches the delegated tasks (SVC-05), that the service plan is individualized to the client's assessed needs and preferences rather than a generic template (SVC-04), and that RN supervisory visits occurred as the plan and client consent require (SVC-06).

Item 3 (coordination of services): the reviewer checks that services delivered match the service plan in type and frequency, that missed visits were handled under SVC-09, that changes in condition were communicated and acted on under SVC-11, and that payer or case manager coordination occurred where applicable (SVC-13).

Item 4 (documentation): the reviewer checks that visit notes, timekeeping, supervisory visit notes, consents and signatures are complete, legible, dated and signed (including valid electronic signatures per REC-01), and that EVV or timekeeping entries match the notes (SVC-10).

Item 5 (policies followed): the reviewer checks key requirements in each record, including rights and hotline notices given on or before the first day of service (CR-03), written service agreement (CR-07), written consent for RN entry into the home, caregiver qualifications and training on file (PER-01, PER-04), and incident reports completed when required (SAF-02).

Item 6 (confidentiality): the reviewer checks that records are stored securely, access is limited to authorized staff, releases of information are on file where needed, and no privacy incident occurred (CR-04). The reviewer also reviews any reported privacy incidents for the quarter.
The reviewer records each finding as met or not met, with a short description and the record reference, on the QA Record Review Form, and signs and dates the form.

Within 10 business days after the review, the reviewer gives the Administrator a written QA summary that includes the number of records reviewed, the findings by item (1 through 7), trends across quarters, and any complaints (CR-02), incidents (SAF-02) and missed visits (SVC-09) for the quarter.

Item 7 (use of findings): for each deficiency or adverse trend, the Administrator assigns a corrective action with a responsible person and due date (for example, staff re-education, record correction, a revised procedure or a change in assignment) and enters it on the QA Corrective Action Log.

Any individual client-record deficiency (for example, a missing signature or an overdue supervisory visit) is corrected promptly in accordance with the agency's late-entry rules, and the correction is noted in the log. Systemic issues are addressed through staff training or policy revision (GOV-06).

At the next quarterly review, the reviewer verifies that prior corrective actions were completed and checks whether they were effective. Open items are carried forward until closed. The log records the verification date and result.

The Administrator reports each quarter's QA summary and corrective actions to the Governing Body (GOV-01) at its next meeting and records the report in the minutes. QA results also feed the annual policy review (GOV-06) and performance improvement priorities (GOV-07).

Findings that suggest abuse, neglect or exploitation are not held for quarterly review. They are reported immediately under SAF-01. Findings that suggest billing irregularities are referred under GOV-08.
QA forms, summaries and corrective action logs are kept for at least [RETENTION PERIOD per REC-01] and are made available to AHCA surveyors on request (GOV-09).

responsibilities.duty: Requires a functioning QA program, receives quarterly QA reports and directs resources for corrective action.
Designates reviewers, ensures a documented review is completed every quarter, assigns and tracks corrective actions, and reports to the Governing Body.
Performs or assists with the clinical portions of the record review and helps correct service plan, delegation and supervision deficiencies.
Selects the sample, completes the review form for items 1-7, writes the QA summary and verifies follow-up.
Document services completely, legibly and on time, cooperate with reviews and carry out assigned corrective actions.

documentation: Quarterly QA Record Review Forms with sample selection method and reviewer signature and date
Quarterly QA summary reports
QA Corrective Action Log with verification of completion
Governing Body minutes showing receipt of QA reports
Designation of QA reviewers

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency license limited to non-skilled services, Homemaker and Companion Services registration (if offered), and all billing to private-pay clients, SMMC LTC plans, APD iBudget, Area Agencies on Aging and other payers
policies.purpose: To prevent fraud, waste and abuse and to make sure [AGENCY NAME] bills only for services that were actually delivered, documented, verified and authorized, and only for services that fall within its license or registration.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] bills only for verified, documented visits that were provided by qualified staff under an authorization or service agreement. The agency does not bill for, advertise or provide any service that is not on its license or registration (s. 400.464, F.S.; s. 400.509, F.S.). Any agency that serves Medicaid managed care members must be screened and enrolled with Florida Medicaid before contracting with SMMC LTC plans (42 CFR 438.602). The agency uses electronic visit verification for Medicaid personal care and home health services as federal law requires (42 U.S.C. 1396b(l); SVC-10). Rates are those in the written client agreement (private pay) or in the written contract with each payer. SMMC LTC rates are negotiated with each plan, so the agency keeps each plan's rate in writing. Fee schedules published under Rule 59G-4.002, F.A.C. are used only where they apply. State-plan personal care under that schedule covers recipients under 21, so it is not assumed to be the rate for adult LTC members. The agency maintains a confidential internal reporting channel and prohibits retaliation against anyone who reports a concern in good faith.

definitions.definition: Knowingly submitting or causing a false claim or statement, such as billing for a visit that did not occur.
Over-use, inaccurate coding or billing practices that cost a payer more than necessary, even without intent to deceive.
A visit supported by EVV or timekeeping data, a signed or electronically authenticated visit note, and an authorization or agreement covering the service, date and hours.
A provider that contracts with an SMMC plan to deliver services to plan members. Network providers must be screened and enrolled with Florida Medicaid (42 CFR 438.602).
The Administrator, or a person the Administrator designates in writing, who oversees this policy.

procedures: The Administrator serves as Compliance Officer unless the Governing Body designates another person in writing. The Compliance Officer's name and contact information are posted for staff.

Before submitting any claim or contracting with an SMMC LTC plan, the Administrator confirms the agency is screened and enrolled with Florida Medicaid and records the enrollment date and Medicaid provider ID in the compliance file. The Administrator also confirms any APD or Area Agency on Aging enrollment or vendor agreement required for those programs.

The Administrator confirms before starting any new service line or payer that the service is within the agency's current license (or registration for homemaker and companion services). Services not on the license or registration are not offered, advertised or billed.

The billing staff member keeps a written rate sheet for each payer. For each SMMC LTC plan, the rate is taken from the signed contract or written rate notice and filed in the payer folder. Rates are never assumed from a public fee schedule. Rate changes are accepted only in writing.

Before any claim is submitted, the billing staff member matches each billed visit to (a) a current authorization or service agreement, (b) an EVV record or timekeeping record, and (c) a signed or electronically authenticated visit note. Visits that fail any match are held and not billed until resolved.

Billing staff may not alter EVV or timekeeping data to make it match a claim. Corrections to EVV data are made only through the system's documented manual-edit process with a reason, the editor's name and the date, and are reviewed by the Administrator (SVC-10).

Claims are submitted at the contracted rate and units actually delivered. Units are not rounded up, and no travel time, missed visit or training time is billed unless the payer contract specifically allows it.

Each month the Compliance Officer reviews a sample of claims against records, looking for visits billed without documentation, overlapping visits for one caregiver, visits billed while a client was hospitalized, and duplicate billing. The results are reported through the QA program (GOV-07).

Employees must be screened as required before any work, and services may not be billed for staff who do not meet qualification, training and background screening requirements at the time of the visit (PER-01 through PER-04).
Clients are given the Medicaid fraud hotline notice and the other required notices on or before the first day of service (CR-03).

Staff report suspected fraud, billing errors or violations of this policy to the Compliance Officer, or, if the concern involves the Compliance Officer, directly to the Governing Body, by phone at [PHONE], by email at [EMAIL], or in writing in a sealed envelope. Reports may be made anonymously.

The Compliance Officer logs each report, begins review within 5 business days, and documents the findings and the actions taken. Suspected fraud against a government program is reported to the proper authority as advised by the Governing Body's legal counsel and as the payer contract requires.

Any overpayment identified is reported to the payer and repaid as the payer contract and law require. The Compliance Officer records the date identified, the amount, the cause and the corrective action.
No employee or contractor is retaliated against for a good-faith report. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination (PER-09).
New employees receive this policy at orientation and acknowledge it in writing (PER-04). All billing and administrative staff review it again each year.
The Governing Body reviews a summary of compliance activity at least annually (GOV-01) and updates this policy through document control (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, receives annual compliance summaries and acts on reports involving the Administrator.
Confirms enrollment and license scope, oversees billing review, receives and investigates reports, and carries out corrective action and repayment.
Bill only verified, authorized, documented visits at written rates and hold any claim that fails a match.
Ensure that visits are delivered as authorized and that records support billing.
Document honestly, never falsify time or notes, and report concerns without fear of retaliation.

documentation: Florida Medicaid enrollment confirmation and provider ID
Signed payer contracts and written rate notices for each SMMC LTC plan and other payer
Monthly claim-to-record audit results
Compliance report log, investigation notes and corrective actions
EVV manual-edit logs
Overpayment and repayment records
Employee acknowledgments of this policy

policies.title: Surveyor Access, Licensure Surveys and Certified Service Verification Reports
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency license limited to non-skilled services; the access and records-retrieval steps also apply to the Homemaker and Companion Services line
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] is ready for the AHCA licensure survey and for unannounced surveys, that surveyors have prompt access to leadership, the client list and records, and that the agency can produce a certified report of services provided by any named staff person within the required time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with AHCA surveys. AHCA surveys before initial licensure and then unannounced at least every 36.9 months (Rule 59A-8.003(2)(a), F.A.C.; s. 400.471(2), F.S.). When a surveyor arrives, the Administrator or alternate is on premises within 1 hour, and a current client list is produced within 2 hours (Rule 59A-8.003(9)(c), F.A.C.). Records must be retrievable during unannounced surveys (Rule 59A-8.022(4), F.A.C.). This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(d), F.A.C.: the agency has a process to verify that personal care services were provided and can produce a certified report of services provided by a named direct-service or contracted staff person for a specified period. The report is due to the surveyor within 2 hours of the request, or within 3 hours if the period requested is longer than one year (Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(d), F.A.C.; s. 400.497(5), F.S.). Because the agency is licensed for non-skilled services only and has no Director of Nursing, the Administrator (or the alternate administrator) performs the production and certification function that the rule assigns to the Director of Nursing.

definitions.definition: A report from the agency's records, certified as accurate by the Administrator or alternate, listing every service visit made by a named direct-service or contracted staff person during a specified period.

A list of all clients currently receiving services, with the information a surveyor needs to select clients for record review and home visits, drawn from the agency's records at the time of the request.
A survey made without advance notice to the agency.
Any employee, CNA, home health aide, RN supervisor or contracted individual who provides services to clients on behalf of the agency.

procedures: The Administrator keeps current at the main office a Survey Readiness Binder (paper or electronic) with the license, insurance certificates, current policy manuals, the emergency management plan, the staff roster and the list of current clients.

The reception staff member is trained to greet any surveyor courteously, ask for identification and the purpose of the visit, note the arrival time on the Survey Log and immediately notify the Administrator or alternate by phone. The surveyor is never refused entry or told to come back later.

If the Administrator is not in the office, the alternate administrator named in GOV-02 is called. Whichever one is notified must be on the premises within 1 hour of the surveyor's arrival. The arrival time and the time of the Administrator's or alternate's arrival are recorded on the Survey Log.
While waiting, staff offer the surveyor a workspace and do not alter, remove or add anything to any client or personnel record.

Within 2 hours of the surveyor's arrival, the Administrator or alternate produces the current client list directly from the client database or records. The agency tests its ability to print or export this list at least quarterly.

The Administrator assigns a staff member to act as the surveyor's escort for record requests, who retrieves client, personnel, training, EVV and policy records promptly and logs each record given to the surveyor and returned.

When a surveyor asks for a certified report of services by a named staff person, the receiving staff member writes down the staff person's name, the period requested and the time of the request, and notifies the Administrator immediately. The 2-hour clock (3 hours if the period exceeds one year) starts at the time of the request.

The Administrator or alternate, with the scheduler, generates the report from EVV or timekeeping data, schedules, visit notes and, if applicable, payroll or contractor invoices. Each entry shows the date, client identifier, start and end times and the service delivered by that named person, and covers the full period requested.
The report is cross-checked against visit notes and EVV records for obvious gaps. Any visit that cannot be verified is listed as unverified. It is not removed from the report.

The Administrator or alternate signs and dates the report with a statement that it was produced from the agency's records and is accurate to the best of his or her knowledge. The report is delivered to the surveyor within the required time. The time of delivery is recorded on the Survey Log.

Staff members who provide direct service are told at orientation that visit documentation and EVV entries may be used to verify their services, and contractors agree to this in their contracts (SVC-15).

Records stored off-site, in a satellite office or in cloud systems must be retrievable promptly during an unannounced survey, and the Administrator confirms access credentials are available to the Administrator and alternate (REC-01).
The agency holds a mock survey at least annually that tests the 1-hour access, 2-hour client list and 2/3-hour service report requirements. Results are entered into the QA program (GOV-07).
At the exit conference the Administrator or alternate attends, takes notes and asks for clarification of any findings.

If a statement of deficiencies is issued, the Administrator prepares a plan of correction by the date stated by AHCA, assigns responsible persons and dates, and documents completion. Corrective actions are tracked through QA (GOV-07).

Before the initial licensure survey, the Administrator confirms that all items on the licensure application, policies, personnel files, client records for any clients served and the emergency plan are complete and available for inspection.

responsibilities.duty: Is on the premises within 1 hour of a surveyor's arrival, produces and certifies the client list and service reports, leads the survey response and prepares any plan of correction.
Performs the Administrator's survey duties when the Administrator is unavailable (GOV-02).
Greet surveyors, log arrival times, notify the Administrator or alternate immediately, and escort and assist the surveyor.
Retrieve records and generate service reports and client lists accurately and quickly.
Is available to answer clinical, delegation and supervision questions and to provide supervisory visit records.

documentation: Survey Log with arrival times, notification times and record requests
Copies of each certified service verification report produced and the time of delivery
Current client list printouts or exports
Mock survey results
Statement of deficiencies, plan of correction and evidence of completion
Survey Readiness Binder checklist

policies.title: Changes of Ownership, Address and Operations; Closure Notices
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency license limited to non-skilled services; Homemaker and Companion Services registration (where noted)
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] reports changes to AHCA on time, protects clients and their records when ownership changes or the agency closes, and does not operate under outdated license or registration information.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports application and insurance changes to AHCA within 21 calendar days (s. 408.810(3), F.S.). It gives AHCA 30 days' notice before discontinuing operation and notifies clients, and it arranges custody of records or publishes notice weekly for 4 consecutive weeks (s. 408.810(4), F.S.). On a change of ownership, client records transfer to the new owner (Rule 59A-8.003(4), F.A.C.). On closure, the license is returned to AHCA (Rule 59A-8.003(10), F.A.C.). A change of address, of counties served, or the opening or closing of an office is filed on AHCA Form 3110-1011 with zoning and right-to-occupy evidence (Rule 59A-8.003(8), F.A.C.). A registered homemaker and companion provider files its renewal or change-of-ownership application at least 60 days before expiration (Rule 59A-8.025(2), F.A.C.). The agency does not operate at a new location, under new ownership or in a new service area until AHCA approval is received where required.

definitions.definition: A transfer of the agency to a new owner or operator as defined by AHCA. A CHOW requires a new application, and the license is not transferable to the new owner.

The counties the agency is licensed to serve, as shown on the license application. For registered homemaker and companion providers, the counties in the health service planning district of the address of record (Rule 59A-8.025(6), F.A.C.).
Closing the agency, or ending a licensed service line, so that clients will no longer receive services from the agency.
A deed, lease or other document showing the agency has the legal right to use the premises (s. 408.810(6), F.S.).

procedures: Any person who learns of a planned or actual change in ownership, address, counties served, administrator, insurance coverage or any other item reported in the application tells the Administrator at once. The Administrator opens a Change Tracking Sheet with the date of the change and the AHCA due date.

Application and insurance changes: the Administrator reports the change to AHCA in writing within 21 calendar days of the change. A copy of the insurance certificate showing the required coverage (GOV-03) is included for any insurance change. The date sent and AHCA's reply are recorded.

Change of address, counties served, or opening or closing of an office: before moving or opening, the Administrator files AHCA Form 3110-1011 with evidence of zoning approval and the legal right to occupy the new premises, and does not begin operating at the new location until AHCA authorizes it. Changes involving a satellite office or drop-off site are handled under GOV-05.

Before an address change, the Administrator also updates the posted license, advertising (including the license or registration number, GOV-03 and GOV-04), client notices, payer and Medicaid enrollment records, insurance, and the hotline and complaint notices given to clients (CR-03).

Change of ownership: the Administrator and the owners identify the planned date, ensure that the new owner files the required application with AHCA, and confirm that the license is not used by the new owner until AHCA issues the new license. The Administrator notifies clients, staff and payers in writing of the change.

On a change of ownership, the Administrator arranges for all client records to transfer to the new owner (Rule 59A-8.003(4), F.A.C.), prepares an inventory of the records, keeps a signed transfer receipt, and protects the privacy of the records during transfer (CR-04, REC-01).
Personnel records, EVV data, payer contracts and Medicaid enrollment are reviewed so they can be transferred or re-established under the new owner without gaps in client services.

Homemaker and companion registration: the Administrator calendars the registration expiration date and files the renewal or change-of-ownership application at least 60 days before it expires (Rule 59A-8.025(2), F.A.C.), using AHCA Form 3110-1003 with the applicable fee. The date filed is recorded in the compliance file.

Planned closure: the Governing Body decides on the closure date. At least 30 days before discontinuing operation, the Administrator gives AHCA written notice (s. 408.810(4), F.S.) and sends a written notice to every client, and to each client's representative, case manager and payer, stating the closure date.

Within the 30 days, the RN Supervisor and the Administrator help each client arrange a transfer to another provider so that no client is left without needed care (SVC-12). Each transfer, and any client who declines, is documented.

The Administrator arranges for custody of client records after closure and gives clients and AHCA the name and address of the custodian. If custody cannot be arranged, the Administrator publishes notice weekly for 4 consecutive weeks as s. 408.810(4), F.S. requires, in a newspaper of general circulation in the area served, and keeps proof of publication.
Records are kept for the full retention period in REC-01 and are not destroyed on closure. Personnel records and financial records are retained as required by law (PER-07).
The Administrator returns the original license to AHCA upon closure (Rule 59A-8.003(10), F.A.C.), keeps a copy and the proof of delivery, and stops all advertising and use of the license number.
Final wages are paid, and staff are informed of the closure date, in accordance with PER-08.
The Administrator reports the change or closure to Medicaid managed care plans, APD, Area Agencies on Aging and other payers as their contracts require, and submits final claims (GOV-08).
A completed Change Tracking Sheet is kept for each event and reviewed by the Governing Body at its next meeting (GOV-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves ownership transfers, address changes and closure, and ensures funding to carry out the notice and record steps.
Tracks deadlines, files reports and applications with AHCA, notifies clients and payers, arranges record custody and returns the license.
Coordinates safe transfer of each client to another provider and documents continuity of care.
Inventory, secure and transfer records and keep proof of transfer or custody.
Files the required applications and does not operate until AHCA approval where required.

documentation: Change Tracking Sheet with AHCA deadlines
Copies of AHCA submissions, including Form 3110-1011 and Form 3110-1003, with proof of delivery
Zoning approval and right-to-occupy evidence
Insurance certificates
Client and payer closure notices
Record transfer inventory and receipt or record custodian agreement
Proof of weekly publication for 4 consecutive weeks, if used
Proof of license return

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All clients of the Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) and, where offered, the Homemaker and Companion Services line, including Medicaid home and community-based services (HCBS) clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows his or her rights and responsibilities, can take part in planning care and is treated with dignity, privacy and respect, with these rights honored in every home.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives each client a written statement of rights and responsibilities and the required notices on or before the first day of service (s. 408.810(5), F.S.). A client has the right to be informed of and participate in care planning and to receive a copy of the plan on request (s. 400.487(4), F.S.; Rule 59A-8.0215(3), F.A.C.). For clients receiving Medicaid HCBS, the agency honors the HCBS settings requirements of choice, privacy, dignity and freedom from coercion (42 CFR 441.301(c); 42 CFR 441.710). A client may refuse the RN supervisory visit, and the RN may enter the home only with the client's written consent (Rule 59A-8.0095(3)(c), F.A.C.). Clients' rights are protected regardless of payer, and staff may not discourage a client from exercising them.

definitions.definition: A person who receives services from [AGENCY NAME], and where applicable the client's representative, guardian or surrogate acting on the client's behalf.
The written plan describing the personal care or other services to be provided to the client (SVC-04). It is the client's plan of care under Rule 59A-8.0215, F.A.C.

Federal requirements for Medicaid home and community-based services under 42 CFR 441.301(c) and 42 CFR 441.710, which include choice, privacy, dignity, respect and freedom from coercion and restraint.
The client's signed permission for the agency's Registered Nurse to enter the home for supervisory visits.

procedures: During intake (SVC-03), and no later than the first day of service, the intake staff member gives the client or representative the Client Rights and Responsibilities statement in plain language, in the client's preferred language, and in large print or read aloud if needed (CR-06).

At the same time, the staff member gives the AHCA complaint notice, the Florida Abuse Hotline notice and the Medicaid fraud hotline notice (s. 408.810(5), F.S.; CR-03). The client or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment that he or she received and understood the notices. The signed form is placed in the client record.
The staff member explains the rights verbally and answers questions. The client is told that the rights apply regardless of payer, race, disability or any other personal characteristic (CR-06).

The client's rights include the right to: be treated with courtesy, dignity and respect; privacy in personal care and in his or her records (CR-04); be free from abuse, neglect, exploitation and restraint (SAF-01); be told what services will be provided, who will provide them and what they will cost (CR-07); take part in planning and changing the service plan and receive a copy on request (s. 400.487(4), F.S.; Rule 59A-8.0215(3), F.A.C.); refuse any service or visit; make a complaint without fear of retaliation (CR-02); and choose among available caregivers where possible.

The client's responsibilities include: giving accurate information about needs and health; telling the agency about changes in condition or schedule; providing a safe work environment free of violence, harassment and hazards (SAF-08); treating caregivers with respect; paying for private-pay services as agreed; and following the service plan.

When the RN Supervisor develops the service plan (SVC-04), the client or representative is told that he or she may take part in developing it and may receive a copy on request. The offer and the client's response are documented in the plan.
If a client asks for a copy of the service plan, a copy is provided promptly at no charge (target: within 2 business days) and the date given is recorded in the record.

For RN supervisory visits (SVC-06), the RN Supervisor explains the purpose of the visit and that the client may agree or refuse, and that supervisory visits are arranged per the client's direction, approval and agreement to pay where applicable (s. 400.487(3), F.S.). The client's written consent to RN entry into the home is obtained and filed before any visit. If the client refuses, the refusal is documented and the RN Supervisor explains the effect on the agency's ability to supervise, and the Administrator and RN determine whether services can continue safely.

For clients receiving Medicaid HCBS, the RN Supervisor confirms that the service plan reflects the client's choices and preferences, that the client's privacy and daily routine are respected, that no restriction on movement, visitors or choices is imposed by staff without a documented plan approved through the payer or case manager, and that staff do not pressure or coerce the client (SVC-13).

Caregivers are trained at orientation and annually on client rights and on honoring them in the home (PER-04). Caregivers report any right they believe is being violated to the RN Supervisor or Administrator.
A client who thinks his or her rights were violated is directed to the grievance process (CR-02). Any report of abuse, neglect or exploitation is handled immediately under SAF-01.
The Administrator reviews QA findings and complaints each quarter for patterns of rights violations and takes corrective action (GOV-07).
The rights statement is reviewed annually through document control (GOV-06) and reissued to clients whenever it changes materially.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every client receives the rights statement and required notices on time, and that violations are investigated and corrected.
Deliver and explain the rights, notices and acknowledgment on or before the first day of service and file the signed acknowledgment.
Involves clients in care planning, offers copies of the plan, obtains written consent for RN entry into the home and verifies HCBS settings protections.

responsibilities.role: Caregivers (CNAs, Home Health Aides, Homemakers and Companions)
responsibilities.duty: Respect client rights during every visit and report suspected violations.

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All clients, family members and representatives of the Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) and the Homemaker and Companion Services line, and all agency staff
policies.purpose: To give clients and their representatives an easy, safe way to raise concerns, to make sure every complaint is recorded, investigated and answered in writing, and to use complaint results to improve services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives every client the AHCA complaint notice on or before the first day of service (s. 408.810(5), F.S.). Each complaint is recorded, investigated and answered in writing, and outcomes are reported through the QA program (GOV-07). The agency never retaliates against a client or employee for filing a complaint, and a client may complain to AHCA at any time without first using the agency's process. For suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, anyone may call the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873, and the agency also reports and acts under SAF-01. Rule 59A-8.0095, F.A.C. requires the agency to follow its own policies, and the agency reviews grievance handling as part of QA.

definitions.definition: Any oral or written expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the services, staff, billing, safety or rights of a client, whether or not the client uses the word 'complaint'.
The confidential record of each complaint, its investigation, response and outcome.
Any adverse action, threat or reduction in service or treatment taken because a person made or supported a complaint.
The Administrator, or the person the Administrator designates in writing to receive and manage complaints.

procedures: On or before the first day of service, the intake staff member gives the client or representative the written complaint procedure and the AHCA complaint notice, with the agency's own contact information ([PHONE], [ADDRESS]) and the name of the Complaint Coordinator, and obtains a signed acknowledgment (CR-03). The notice is given in the client's language or format (CR-06).

Clients and representatives may complain by phone, in person, in writing, by email or through any staff member, and may do so anonymously. No form is required, and any staff member who receives a complaint accepts it.

The staff member who receives a complaint writes down the date, the name of the client, the details and the name of the complainant and gives it to the Complaint Coordinator by the end of the next business day. A complaint that involves a risk to health or safety is reported to the Complaint Coordinator immediately.

If a complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member follows SAF-01 at once, including calling the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873. The complaint process does not delay or replace the required report.
The Complaint Coordinator enters the complaint in the Complaint Log and acknowledges it to the complainant, in writing or by phone, within 2 business days.

The Complaint Coordinator investigates promptly by reviewing records, speaking to the client, caregiver and RN Supervisor, and checking EVV or schedule data. The investigation is started within 2 business days, and any immediate safety issue is addressed first, for example by reassigning the caregiver.

A caregiver or staff member who is the subject of a complaint is not told to retaliate and does not investigate his or her own complaint. If the complaint involves the Administrator, the Governing Body designates another person to investigate.

The Complaint Coordinator completes the investigation and gives the complainant a written response within 14 calendar days. If more time is needed, the complainant is told why and given a new date, and the matter is completed within 30 calendar days. The response states the findings, the action taken and how to appeal or contact outside agencies.

The written response always tells the complainant that he or she may contact AHCA at the number on the complaint notice [AHCA COMPLAINT HOTLINE NUMBER as printed on the current AHCA notice], the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 for abuse, neglect or exploitation, and the Medicaid fraud hotline for suspected fraud [MEDICAID FRAUD HOTLINE NUMBER as printed on the current notice].

Where the client's services are paid by an SMMC LTC plan, the APD iBudget, or an Area Agency on Aging, the Complaint Coordinator also notifies the client's case manager or care coordinator when the complaint involves services they authorized, as the payer contract requires (SVC-13).

If the complaint is substantiated, the Complaint Coordinator documents the corrective action, for example coaching, retraining, reassignment, discipline (PER-09) or a change in procedure, and confirms it was completed.

No client, family member or employee is retaliated against for making a complaint. Staff who retaliate are subject to discipline up to termination. A client's services are not reduced or ended because of a complaint.
If the client is dissatisfied with the outcome, the client may ask for review by the Administrator or Governing Body, and the review is completed within 14 calendar days.

The Complaint Coordinator reports to the Administrator each month and to the QA reviewer each quarter on the number, types, timeliness and outcomes of complaints, with trends by caregiver, service and payer (GOV-07).
Complaints that involve a reportable incident are also documented under SAF-02, and any complaint made by AHCA or another regulator is handled under GOV-09.
Complaint records are kept confidential (CR-04) and retained under REC-01. Surveyors may review them on request.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews complaint trends and investigates any complaint about the Administrator.
Logs, investigates and responds in writing to every complaint, ensures no retaliation and reports outcomes through QA.
Helps investigate clinical and care-related complaints and implements corrective action in care and supervision.
Accept any complaint, report it to the Complaint Coordinator by the next business day, and never discourage or retaliate against a complainant.

documentation: Signed client acknowledgment of the complaint procedure and AHCA complaint notice
Complaint Log with dates received, acknowledged, investigated and closed
Investigation notes and written responses
Corrective action records
Monthly complaint reports to the Administrator and quarterly QA summaries
Records of referrals to the Florida Abuse Hotline or other agencies, if made

policies.title: Required Hotline and Complaint Notices at Start of Service
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, schedulers, RN Supervisor, home health aides/CNAs, homemaker and companion staff, Administrator, and all clients and client representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every client receives the required complaint, abuse hotline and Medicaid fraud hotline notices on or before the first day of service, and to give the surveyor the written policy that s. 408.810(5), F.S. requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives each client, on or before the first day of service, the complaint, Florida Abuse Hotline and Medicaid fraud hotline notices required by s. 408.810(5), F.S. This is the agency's written policy for giving those notices. The notices use the current text and telephone numbers supplied by the Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA). The Florida Abuse Hotline number is 1-800-962-2873. No first visit is released to a caregiver until the notice acknowledgment is in the client record. This policy applies to every service line: licensed non-skilled home health aide services and companion/homemaker services.

definitions.definition: The AHCA complaint notice, the Florida Abuse Hotline notice, and the Medicaid fraud hotline notice that s. 408.810(5), F.S. requires licensees to give each client.
The date of the first visit by any agency caregiver to the client. The notices are due on or before that date.
The legal guardian, health care surrogate, agent under a power of attorney, or other person legally authorized to act for the client.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a current copy of the AHCA-provided complaint, abuse hotline and Medicaid fraud hotline notices in the policy manual and in the intake packet. The Administrator checks the notice text and telephone numbers against AHCA's current notice at each annual policy review (GOV-06) and whenever AHCA announces a change.
The intake coordinator places the notices in every admission packet, in the client's primary language or in a format the client can use (see CR-06).

At or before the first visit, the intake coordinator or RN Supervisor gives the client or client representative the notices in writing. The coordinator explains in plain language that the client may call these numbers at any time and that the agency will not retaliate for a call.

If the client cannot read the notice because of vision, literacy or language, staff read it aloud or use an interpreter, large print or translation technology, and document how the notice was delivered.
The client or representative signs and dates the Notice Acknowledgment. Staff give the client a copy of the notices and the signed acknowledgment, and file the original in the client record.

If the client or representative cannot sign or declines to sign, the staff member writes the reason on the acknowledgment form, signs and dates it, and leaves the notices with the client. The RN Supervisor or Administrator reviews the entry within one business day.
If the first contact is an emergency or after-hours start, staff give the notices at the first visit. The Administrator's designee confirms by the next business day that the acknowledgment is filed.

The scheduler does not confirm the first visit to the caregiver until the intake coordinator marks 'Required Notices Given' in the client record. If the notice cannot be delivered ahead of time, the intake coordinator hands the packet to the caregiver and the caregiver delivers and documents it at the first visit.
The agency posts the same notices in the office where clients and visitors can see them, with the agency's own grievance contact [PHONE] (see CR-02).

Staff give the notices again whenever AHCA changes them or a client or representative asks. A client who changes service lines, for example from companion to aide care, does not need new notices unless the text has changed, but the record must show the first-day delivery.

Orientation (PER-04) teaches every caregiver what the notices say, how to answer a client's questions about them, and that caregivers may not discourage, delay or screen a client's call. Caregivers must report any client request for a hotline number to the supervisor on the same day, but may never block a client from calling.
Caregivers who suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation report it to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 as set out in SAF-01. This policy does not replace that duty.

Each quarter the QA coordinator audits a sample of new admissions (at least 10 files or all new files if fewer) for a signed acknowledgment dated on or before the first service date. The results go to the QA committee (GOV-07). Any missing acknowledgment is corrected within two business days, and the cause is recorded.
The Administrator makes the policy and sample notices available to the AHCA surveyor on request (GOV-09).

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, keeps the notices current, reviews exceptions and acts on audit findings.
Packages and delivers the notices, obtains the signed acknowledgment, and files it before first service.
Does not release a first visit until the record shows the notices were given.
Reviews notice delivery for aide clients during assessment and resolves refusals or unable-to-sign entries.
Deliver the notices when assigned, never obstruct a client's use of the hotlines, and report abuse as required.
Audits files quarterly and reports to the QA committee.

documentation: Signed and dated Notice Acknowledgment in each client record
Intake checklist entry 'Required Notices Given' with date and staff initials
Notes on refusal or inability to sign
Current AHCA notice text kept in the policy manual with the date last verified
Quarterly audit results and corrective actions

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted staff, volunteers, students and the Administrator; all client records in paper and electronic form
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client information, to disclose it only as Florida rules and HIPAA allow, and to give clients their privacy rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps all client information confidential. The agency does not disclose client information without the written consent of the client or guardian (Rule 59A-8.022(2), F.A.C.). Client records are confidential and exempt from Chapter 119, F.S. The confidential client record kept for homemaker and companion services is also confidential (Rule 59A-8.025(8), F.A.C.). On request, the agency transfers a copy of the record to another agency (Rule 59A-8.022(3), F.A.C.). The agency follows the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), gives each client its Notice of Privacy Practices (45 CFR 164.520), and meets the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530, including a designated privacy official, staff training at hire and annually, safeguards, a complaint process and sanctions. Where Florida rule and HIPAA both apply, the agency follows the stricter protection for the client.

definitions.definition: Identifiable information about a client's health, care or payment for care, in any form (paper, electronic or spoken).
A signed and dated document in which the client or guardian permits a stated disclosure to a named person or organization.
The written notice describing how the agency uses and discloses PHI and the client's rights, as required by 45 CFR 164.520.
The person the Administrator designates to develop and carry out privacy policies and receive privacy complaints: [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME].

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer in writing, lists the name and [PHONE] in the Notice of Privacy Practices and posts it in the office.

At or before the first service, the intake coordinator gives each client or representative the agency's Notice of Privacy Practices, asks for a signed and dated acknowledgment, and files it in the record. If the client does not sign, staff document the good-faith effort and the reason.

Staff obtain a signed, dated written consent or authorization before disclosing client information to anyone not otherwise allowed by law, including family members not named as representatives, other agencies, physicians, employers or the media. The authorization names the recipient, the information, the purpose and an expiration date, and the record keeps a copy.
Staff follow the 'minimum necessary' rule: caregivers see only the information they need for the assigned client, and office staff access only the records their jobs require.

Staff do not discuss clients in public places, on social media, in text messages containing identifiers, or with anyone without a need to know. Care instructions to caregivers are sent only through the agency's approved secure channels.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in a locked room at [ADDRESS]. Electronic records are protected with unique user IDs, passwords, automatic log-off, access logs, encryption where available and backup, consistent with REC-01. Caregivers bring only the client's care plan and schedule into the home and return or shred it as the supervisor directs.

When another agency or provider asks for a copy of a client's record in connection with a transfer, the Records Clerk verifies the request and the client's consent, and sends a copy of the record promptly, no later than three business days after the request. The transfer is logged in the record.

The agency produces records for an AHCA surveyor during a licensure survey as required by law (GOV-09). Subpoenas, court orders and other legal requests go to the Administrator before any release. Staff do not release records on their own judgment.
Staff treat the homemaker/companion confidential client record (REC-02) the same as any other client record and do not share its contents without written consent.

Clients may ask to see or get a copy of their records, to request corrections, to request an accounting of disclosures and to request restrictions. The Privacy Officer responds in writing within the time HIPAA allows and documents the response.

Clients may complain about privacy practices to the Privacy Officer at [PHONE], to the agency's grievance process (CR-02) or to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The agency does not retaliate against anyone who complains.

The Privacy Officer trains every new employee on this policy during orientation (PER-04) before the employee has access to client information, and retrains all staff at least annually. Training is documented with date, topic, trainer and signed attendance.

A staff member who suspects an impermissible use or disclosure reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the work day. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits harm, decides whether the breach rule requires notice to the client and federal authorities, and documents the result.
Staff who violate this policy are subject to discipline up to termination, applied consistently and documented in the personnel record.
Business associates and vendors who handle PHI, such as billing, software and storage vendors, must have signed agreements with the agency before they receive any PHI.
The Privacy Officer keeps HIPAA policies, training records, complaints and breach documentation for at least six years and reviews this policy at least annually (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Privacy Officer, approves this policy, enforces discipline and receives legal requests.
Administers the privacy program, handles complaints and breaches, and conducts training.
Provides the Notice of Privacy Practices and obtains consents and acknowledgments.
Controls access, processes record transfer requests and keeps the disclosure log.
Maintain confidentiality, disclose only as authorized, and report suspected breaches immediately.

documentation: Signed Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgment
Signed written consents/authorizations for disclosure
Record transfer log with date requested and date sent
Disclosure log and client requests for access, amendment and restrictions
Privacy complaints and breach investigations
Staff HIPAA training records at hire and annually
Business associate agreements

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (home health aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions), schedulers, supervisors and office staff
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property and money, prevent financial exploitation of clients, and make sure any money handled for errands is tracked.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires respect for each client's privacy and property, as taught in aide training (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c) topic 8, F.A.C.). Caregivers may not borrow money from clients, accept gifts, become a beneficiary of a client, or handle a client's credit/debit cards or checks. Any shopping or errand money is documented with receipts and a signed log. Suspected exploitation of a vulnerable adult is reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 (see SAF-01). Clients receive the hotline notices described in CR-03 (s. 408.810(5), F.S.).

definitions.definition: Improper use of a client's funds, property or assets, including theft, undue influence, coercion or deception, for the benefit of someone other than the client.
Money, goods, services, loans, tips or favors from a client or the client's family to a caregiver or other agency staff.
Cash that a client gives a caregiver to buy items for the client, which must be handled under the signed log in this policy.
A person named to receive property, money or other benefit from a client, such as in a will, trust, insurance policy, account or power of attorney arrangement.

procedures: At hire and in orientation (PER-04), each caregiver receives this policy, signs that they have read it, and completes the aide training topic on respect for client privacy and property.

The intake coordinator explains the policy to the client and family at admission and states in the service agreement (CR-07) that caregivers may not accept gifts, loans or tips and cannot handle cards or checks.

Caregivers may not borrow money or property, sell items to or buy items from a client, accept gifts or tips, or be named as a beneficiary, agent, joint account holder, trustee or witness for any client document.
If a client offers a gift, the caregiver politely declines, explains that agency policy prohibits it, and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor documents the offer in the client record.
Caregivers do not use, hold, sign or carry a client's credit cards, debit cards, checks, PINs, bank account information or online banking login information, even if the client asks.

When a client wants an errand or shopping done, the supervisor approves it in the service plan (SVC-04). The caregiver and client count the cash and record the amount on the Errand Money Log, and both sign it. The client signs again when the caregiver returns with the purchases, receipt and change.
The caregiver keeps all receipts, keeps client cash separate from personal money, never uses client funds for personal purchases, and returns change and receipts at the same visit whenever possible.

The supervisor reviews each Errand Money Log and receipts at least weekly for active errand clients and compares them to the plan. Discrepancies are reported to the Administrator within one business day.

Caregivers do not move, remove, sell, pawn, lend or use a client's belongings, vehicle or home for personal benefit, and do not access a client's mail or financial papers unless the service plan specifically directs it.

Caregivers report missing or damaged client property to the supervisor immediately. The supervisor completes an incident report (SAF-02) the same day, and the Administrator reviews the facts and notifies the client or representative.

Any employee who suspects financial exploitation of a client, by staff, family or others, reports it directly to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 as required in SAF-01 and notifies the Administrator. Reporting does not wait for an internal investigation.
The Administrator removes any caregiver under investigation for exploitation from the client's case while the investigation continues, and keeps client safety and non-retaliation as priorities.
The agency reports substantiated cases to the appropriate authorities and applies discipline, up to termination, as documented in the personnel record (PER-09).
The QA coordinator reviews property complaints, errand logs and exploitation concerns quarterly and reports trends to the QA committee (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the policy, investigates reports and ensures hotline reports are made.
Approve errands, review logs, document gift offers and respond to property complaints.
Follow all prohibitions, keep logs and receipts, and report concerns immediately.
Explain the policy to clients and families at admission.

documentation: Caregiver signed acknowledgment of this policy
Signed Errand Money Logs with receipts
Client record notes of declined gifts
Incident reports for missing or damaged property
Abuse Hotline report confirmation numbers
Investigation and discipline records
Service agreement language on gifts and handling of cards and checks

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff involved in intake, admission, scheduling, care delivery and billing; all clients and applicants
policies.purpose: To make sure clients are treated without discrimination, that people with disabilities and limited English proficiency can understand and take part in their care, and that the agency accepts only clients it can communicate with and serve safely.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate against any client or applicant on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, age, disability or any other basis prohibited by law, in accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. 12101 et seq.) and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. 2000d). The agency accepts a client only when services can reasonably be provided safely in the home, including the ability to communicate through a same-language staff person, an interpreter or translation technology (Rule 59A-8.020(1), F.A.C.). The agency does not condition admission or treatment on whether a client has an advance directive (Rule 59A-8.0245(1), F.A.C.; see CR-08). The agency provides aids and services to clients with disabilities at no charge. Aide training covers cultural differences in families (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c) topic 13, F.A.C.).

definitions.definition: A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to take part in care without language help.
An employee who speaks the client's language and is able to communicate accurately with the client in that language.
Qualified telephone, video or software interpretation or translation tools the agency uses when staff or an interpreter are not available.
Items or services that allow people with disabilities to communicate and take part, such as sign language interpreters, large print, Braille, captioning or text-to-speech tools.

procedures: At the first contact, the intake coordinator asks the client's preferred spoken and written language and any communication needs, including hearing, vision, speech, cognitive or literacy needs, and records the answers in the intake record.

Before accepting a client, the intake coordinator and RN Supervisor confirm that the agency can communicate with the client and can staff every assigned visit through a same-language caregiver, an interpreter or translation technology (Rule 59A-8.020(1), F.A.C.). The decision is recorded in the intake record.

If the agency cannot meet the client's language needs, the intake coordinator does not admit the client, offers help finding another provider, and documents the referral. The reason is communication or staffing capacity, not the client's national origin or any other protected trait.
The agency never asks or allows a client to use a minor child as an interpreter. Family members or friends interpret only if the client requests it, and the request is documented.

The agency gives the required notices (CR-03), service agreement (CR-07), client rights (CR-01) and privacy notice (CR-04) in the client's language or reads and explains them using an interpreter or translation technology. The record notes how each was delivered.

The Administrator maintains a current list of bilingual staff with language skills verified by a documented check, interpreter services, and translation technology, and makes it available to the intake coordinator and scheduler.

The agency provides auxiliary aids and services for clients with disabilities at no charge to the client, including large-print documents, readers, sign language interpreters and accessible formats, and documents what was provided.
The agency evaluates requests for reasonable modifications of its policies for clients with disabilities on an individual basis. The Administrator decides and records the outcome and reasons.

The agency does not refuse, limit or end services, assign lower-quality care, or set different terms because of a protected characteristic. Caregiver assignment may consider the client's stated preference only where it relates to personal care needs, language or safety and is documented, and must not result in unlawful discrimination.
Admission decisions are based on the criteria in SVC-03: client need, ability to provide safe service, and staff capacity.
The agency does not condition admission or treatment on advance-directive status, and intake staff do not ask about it as an eligibility question (CR-08).
The agency posts a notice of nondiscrimination and language assistance in the office and includes it in the admission packet.

A client or representative who believes they were discriminated against may file a grievance under CR-02. The Administrator investigates, responds in writing and protects the complainant from retaliation.

The Administrator trains all staff at hire and annually on this policy, working with interpreters and cultural differences in families, consistent with aide training topic 13, and documents the training (PER-04).
The QA committee reviews language-access needs, interpreter use, denials of admission and discrimination grievances at least annually (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures nondiscrimination compliance, keeps language resources current, and investigates complaints.
Screens language and communication needs and documents admission decisions.
Assigns same-language caregivers or arranges interpreters for every visit.
Confirms communication capacity for aide clients and addresses accessibility during assessment.
Treat clients respectfully and without discrimination and use language services.

documentation: Intake record of language and communication needs
Admission decision with reason, including referrals when not accepted
Interpreter or translation technology use, and auxiliary aids provided
Client request to use a family member as interpreter
Bilingual staff and interpreter list
Training attendance records
Discrimination grievances and outcomes

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, RN Supervisor, billing staff, Administrator, caregivers, clients and client representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every client receives a signed written agreement at the start of services that discloses services, rates and payment sources, and to establish the agreement as the service provision plan where no practitioner's treatment order exists.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-8.020(2), F.A.C. At the start of services, [AGENCY NAME] enters into a written agreement with the client or legal representative that includes the information required by s. 400.487(1), F.S.: the services to be provided, the rates for privately paid services and the payment sources. The agreement is signed and dated by an agency representative and by the client or representative. A copy goes to the client and the original is kept in the client file. This policy also meets Rule 59A-8.020(3), F.A.C. For homemaker and companion clients, and for home health aide clients who do not need a practitioner's treatment order, the written agreement serves as the service provision plan under s. 400.491(2), F.S. The agency keeps it for one year after services end. The agreement also states minimum shift lengths, cancellation terms and the terms for RN supervisory-visit consent and payment.

definitions.definition: The written agreement between the agency and the client or representative stating services, rates, payment sources and other terms of care.
For aide, homemaker and companion clients without a treatment order, the service agreement, which serves as the plan of services under s. 400.491(2), F.S. and Rule 59A-8.020(3), F.A.C.
Services paid for by the client or family rather than by Medicaid, a managed care plan or another third-party payer.
A visit by the agency's registered nurse to the client's home to supervise aide services, arranged per the client's direction, approval and agreement to pay for the visits (s. 400.487(3), F.S.).

procedures: Before the first visit, the intake coordinator and the RN Supervisor (for aide clients) review the proposed services, schedule and rates with the client or representative in plain language and in the client's language (CR-06).

The intake coordinator prepares the service agreement on the agency's approved form. The agreement lists each service to be provided (aide personal care, homemaker or companion), the rates for privately paid services and the payment source or sources for each service, such as private pay, long-term care insurance, a Medicaid managed care plan or an agency contract.

The agreement states the minimum shift length, rates for holidays, overnight or live-in service if offered, mileage or transport charges if any, the invoicing and payment schedule, late payment terms and refund terms, so there are no undisclosed charges.

The agreement states cancellation terms: how much notice the client must give, any charge for late cancellation or missed visit, and how the agency will notify the client of its own cancellations (SVC-09).

For aide clients, the agreement describes RN supervisory visits to the home and the client's right to direct and approve them. It states the client's written consent for the RN to enter the home and the client's agreement on payment for the visits, including the rate or that the visit is included in the rate, consistent with SVC-06.

The agreement tells the client of the right to take part in care planning and to receive a copy of the plan on request (s. 400.487(4), F.S.; see SVC-04) and of the agency's grievance process (CR-02) and hotline notices (CR-03).

For clients served through Medicaid or another payer, the agreement identifies the payer, states that the agency bills the payer for authorized services, and states that the client owes only what the payer allows. The agency does not bill the client for payer-covered services (SVC-13, GOV-08).

For homemaker and companion clients and aide clients with no practitioner's treatment order, the agreement is written to serve as the service provision plan: it includes the specific services, frequency, duration and any limits on tasks (SVC-01, SVC-02, SVC-04). The RN Supervisor reviews aide agreements before signature.

An agency representative with authority to bind the agency and the client or representative sign and date the agreement before services start. Electronic signatures follow REC-01. If the client cannot sign, the legal representative signs and the record shows the representative's authority.
The intake coordinator gives the client or representative a complete copy of the signed agreement on the date of signature and documents the delivery. The original is filed in the client record.

Any change in services, schedule, rates or payer requires an amended agreement or written addendum, signed and dated by both parties, and the client receives a copy. The agency gives clients at least 30 days' written notice before a private-pay rate increase, unless the client requests a service change.

Billing staff issue invoices that match the agreement, show dates, hours, services and rates, and are consistent with the agency's time records (SVC-10). The billing staff answer billing questions within three business days and refer disputes to the Administrator as grievances under CR-02.

The agency keeps the agreement for one year after services end for homemaker, companion and non-treatment-order aide clients, as the service provision plan (Rule 59A-8.020(3), F.A.C.). The Records Clerk applies the longer retention period in REC-01 if that policy requires one.
Each quarter the QA coordinator audits new agreements for required content, signatures and dates, copy to client and consistency with services provided, and reports to the QA committee (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement form and rates and ensures agreements comply with this policy.
Prepares and explains the agreement, obtains signatures and gives the client a copy.
Reviews aide agreements and obtains the client's RN-visit consent and payment terms.
Bill only per the agreement and authorized payer terms, and respond to billing questions.
Files originals and keeps them for the required retention period.

documentation: Signed and dated service agreement (original in the client file, copy to the client)
Documentation of date the client received the copy
Signed addenda for changes in services, rates or payer
Client consent for the RN to enter the home and agreement on payment for supervisory visits
Invoices and billing correspondence
Quarterly agreement audit results

policies.title: Advance Directives and Do Not Resuscitate Orders
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, RN Supervisor, caregivers (home health aides/CNAs, homemakers, companions), Administrator, and all adult clients
federal: 42 CFR 489.102 (not applicable unless Medicare-certified; included for reference only)
policies.purpose: To state the agency's position on Florida advance-directive law, make sure adult clients receive required written information before services begin, document directives in the record, and make sure CPR is withheld only on a valid Do Not Resuscitate Order.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0245(1), F.A.C. [AGENCY NAME] respects the right of each adult client under Florida law to make health care decisions, including the right to accept or refuse care and to execute an advance directive. The agency's position is that it will honor valid advance directives and a valid Do Not Resuscitate Order (DNRO) as Florida law requires. The agency never conditions treatment or admission on whether the individual has executed or waived an advance directive. Conflicts between the agency's policies and a client's advance directive are handled under Chapter 765, F.S. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0245(2)(a), (2)(b) and (2)(c), F.A.C., on written information and record documentation, and Rule 59A-8.0245(3), F.A.C., and s. 400.487(7), F.S., on DNROs. Agency personnel may withhold or withdraw cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) only when a valid DNRO executed under s. 401.45, F.S. is present.

definitions.definition: A written or oral statement of a person's wishes about medical care, such as a living will or designation of a health care surrogate, under Chapter 765, F.S.
An order on the Florida Department of Health form, executed under s. 401.45, F.S., directing that CPR be withheld or withdrawn. A living will or health care surrogate designation is not a DNRO.
A person designated by the client to make health care decisions if the client cannot.
'Health Care Advance Directives – The Patients' Right to Decide' (AHCA, rev. April 2006), or an equivalent written description of Florida law.

procedures: Agency position (Rule 59A-8.0245(1)): The Administrator maintains this policy as the agency's written statement of its position. Staff explain it to clients as follows: the agency honors valid advance directives and valid DNROs, never requires a directive for admission or care, and will not penalize anyone for having or not having one.

Admission is never conditioned on, and no staff member asks about advance directives as an eligibility question. The intake coordinator asks about directives only to provide information and make the record (CR-06).

Required booklet (Rule 59A-8.0245(2)(a)): Before services begin, the intake coordinator gives each adult client a copy of 'Health Care Advance Directives – The Patients' Right to Decide' (AHCA, rev. April 2006) or an equivalent written description of Florida law. The Administrator checks at each annual review (GOV-06) that the version in the admission packet is current and accurate.

Agency policy information (Rule 59A-8.0245(2)(b)): Before services begin, the intake coordinator gives each adult client the written Advance Directive Policy Statement, which summarizes this policy, including how the agency treats DNROs and what caregivers will do in an emergency.

The client or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment that both documents were received. If the client is incapacitated, the information is given to the representative. If the client cannot sign, staff document why.

Record documentation (Rule 59A-8.0245(2)(c)): At intake, the intake coordinator records in the client record whether the client has executed an advance directive, using the Advance Directive Status form (yes, no, or not known).

If the client has a directive, staff ask for a copy and place it in the client record. If no copy is received, staff document the date and method of the request and follow up once at the first RN supervisory visit or reassessment.

The agency does not hold itself out as a witness, surrogate or agent for any client, and staff do not witness or sign advance directives for clients (CR-05). The agency may give clients general written information or tell them where to get forms, but it does not give legal advice.

DNRO (Rule 59A-8.0245(3); s. 400.487(7)): If the client has a DNRO, the RN Supervisor verifies that it is on the Florida Department of Health form, has been signed as required and is the valid version, and places a copy in the record. The service plan notes its location in the home (SVC-04) and the caregiver is told where it is kept.

In a cardiac or respiratory arrest, the caregiver immediately calls 911. If a valid DNRO is in the home and available, the caregiver shows it to the responding personnel and withholds CPR as the DNRO directs. If no valid DNRO can be found immediately, the caregiver begins CPR as trained and continues until emergency personnel take over. A living will, surrogate designation or family request alone is not a DNRO.

The caregiver notifies the supervisor immediately after any emergency. The supervisor ensures the Administrator is told, an incident report is completed (SAF-02) and the client's representative is informed (SVC-11).

Conflicts: If the client's directive or wishes conflict with the agency's policy, or if the client, family and surrogate disagree about care, the RN Supervisor notifies the Administrator the same day. The Administrator handles the conflict under Chapter 765, F.S., respects the client's rights, and, if the agency cannot honor the directive, arranges transfer to another provider under SVC-12. The agency does not abandon clients.

Changes: A client may revoke or change a directive or DNRO at any time. Staff who learn of a change notify the RN Supervisor, who updates the record, the service plan and the in-home information the same day.

Training: Orientation and annual in-service training (PER-04) cover this policy, how to recognize a valid DNRO, the caregiver's emergency steps, and current CPR (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(k), F.A.C., requires current CPR). Attendance is recorded.

The Administrator reviews this policy and the Florida forms and booklet used in the packet at least annually, and when the rule or the Department of Health form changes (GOV-06). The QA coordinator audits new admissions quarterly for the required documents and status entries (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the agency's position, keeps forms current and resolves conflicts under Chapter 765, F.S.
Gives the booklet and policy statement before services begin and records directive status.
Verifies DNROs, follows up for copies of directives and updates service plans.
Know where the DNRO is kept, call 911, follow the DNRO or begin CPR as trained, and report immediately.
Audits files for required documentation.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment that the AHCA booklet (or equivalent) and agency policy information were received before services began
Advance Directive Status form in the client record
Copy of any advance directive and DNRO in the record, or note of request for copy and date
Service plan note on DNRO location
Incident reports for emergencies
Training records
Conflict resolution notes

policies.title: Scope of Services — What Home Health Aides and CNAs May and May Not Do
