policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides non-skilled services only: hands-on personal care by home health aides and CNAs under RN supervision. The agency does not provide skilled nursing, physical therapy or other skilled services and does not use LPNs. A non-skilled agency is exempt from the accreditation requirement (s. 400.471, F.S.) and does not need a director of nursing (DON) (s. 400.476, F.S.; Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(i), F.A.C.). The agency may not add skilled services or LPNs until it has completed the steps in this policy. Adding skilled care requires an 'Addition of Skilled Care Services' application to AHCA, accreditation within 120 days, a DON, and a 24-hour on-call system. This policy meets the following official checklist items, which apply only if the agency becomes a skilled agency or uses LPNs. (1) Rule 59A-8.003(9)(d)-1, 24-hour availability: if skilled services are added, [AGENCY NAME] will maintain written policies and procedures for 24-hour availability of licensed professional nursing staff to active skilled clients, with an on-call system in which designated nursing staff can communicate directly with the client (Procedures 8-9). (2) Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(a)4, manuals: the DON would maintain and adhere to the agency procedure and client care policy manuals. This is not required today because no DON is needed without skilled care, and until then the administrator maintains the manuals under GOV-06 (Procedure 7). (3) Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(b), biomedical waste: if nursing or physical therapy services are provided, the DON, administrator or alternate administrator will establish biomedical waste policies and procedures (Procedure 10, building on SAF-04). (4) Rule 59A-8.0095(4)(a), LPN evaluation: if LPNs are used, the RN will evaluate each LPN's performance of duties at least annually, and the evaluation will be documented in the personnel file (Procedure 11).

definitions.definition: Services that require a licensed nurse or therapist, such as skilled nursing or physical therapy, as opposed to personal care by aides.
An agency licensed under Part III of Chapter 400, F.S., limited to non-skilled services such as hands-on personal care by home health aides and CNAs.
A registered nurse required to direct nursing services in an agency that provides skilled care.
A licensed practical nurse. The agency does not currently use LPNs.

definitions.term: Addition of Skilled Care Services application
definitions.definition: The application an AHCA-licensed non-skilled agency must file to add skilled services to its license.

procedures: The administrator confirms at each annual policy review that the agency provides no skilled nursing, therapy or LPN services, and records the confirmation in the policy review log (GOV-06).
Staff may not accept a referral that requires skilled services. Intake staff refer such clients to a licensed skilled provider and document the referral (SVC-03).
The administrator confirms that advertising, the service agreement and the service plan describe only non-skilled services (GOV-03, CR-07).
The governing body must vote to add skilled services or LPNs, and the vote is recorded in its minutes. No skilled service or LPN may be used before the steps below are complete.

If skilled services are approved, the administrator files the 'Addition of Skilled Care Services' application with AHCA and pays the required fee. The agency begins skilled services only after AHCA approves the change.
The agency will obtain accreditation within 120 days as required for skilled agencies and keep the accreditation documents in the compliance file.

Before skilled services start, the agency will hire a qualified DON. The DON will maintain and adhere to the agency procedure and client care policy manuals (Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(a)4) and sign the manuals at each review.

Before skilled services start, the administrator and DON will adopt written policies and procedures for 24-hour availability of licensed professional nursing staff to active skilled clients (Rule 59A-8.003(9)(d)).

The 24-hour policy will describe an on-call system with a posted rotation, a phone number given to each skilled client, and direct communication between the client and the designated on-call nursing staff. The on-call nurse will log each call.

Before skilled nursing or physical therapy starts, the DON, administrator or alternate administrator will establish biomedical waste policies and procedures (Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(b)), expanding SAF-04 to cover skilled care waste.

If LPNs are used, the RN will evaluate each LPN's performance of duties at least once a year, using a written tool, and file the evaluation in the personnel file (Rule 59A-8.0095(4)(a)). The agency will also add LPN supervision to SVC-05 and SVC-06.

The administrator will update the license application information about services and staff, reflecting services provided directly by employees and by contract (SVC-15), and report operational changes under GOV-10.
The administrator will train staff on the revised policies before the first skilled client is admitted and record the training (PER-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether to add skilled services or LPNs and records the decision in its minutes.
Confirms the non-skilled scope annually, files any application to add skilled care, and updates policies.
Maintains the manuals, oversees the 24-hour on-call system and biomedical waste policy, and ensures annual LPN evaluations.
Screens referrals for skilled needs and, if LPNs are used, completes their annual evaluations.
Declines and refers skilled referrals.

documentation: Annual scope confirmation in the policy review log
Referral-out records for skilled needs
Governing body minutes on any proposed addition
AHCA 'Addition of Skilled Care Services' application and approval, if any
Accreditation documents, if any
24-hour on-call policy, rotation and call logs, if any
Biomedical waste policy, if any
LPN annual evaluations in personnel files, if any

policies.title: Services to Residents of Assisted Living Facilities and Adult Family Care Homes; Contracted Staff
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake coordinator, RN supervisor, scheduling staff, and caregivers who serve residents of assisted living facilities (ALFs) and adult family care homes, and any contracted staff
policies.purpose: To make sure services to residents of ALFs and adult family care homes are coordinated with the facility, that [AGENCY NAME] stays responsible for its own services, and that contracted and employed services are clearly identified.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may contract directly with a resident of an assisted living facility or adult family care home to provide non-skilled home health aide services. When it does, the agency coordinates with the facility and remains responsible for the services it provides (Rule 59A-8.008(5), F.A.C.). The agency accepts such a resident only when services can reasonably be provided safely and all assigned visits can be assured (Rule 59A-8.020(1), F.A.C.). The agency will not rely on facility staff to deliver agency services. If the agency's office is located in space within an ALF, the agency will notify AHCA in writing (Rule 59A-8.008(6)). The agency states in its license application which services are provided directly by employees and which are provided by contract, and it provides at least one service directly to clients (Rule 59A-8.008(4)). The agency documents each facility's evacuation plan for each resident it serves. Contracted caregivers must meet the same qualification, screening, training, supervision and documentation requirements as employees.

definitions.definition: A licensed residential facility that provides housing, meals and personal assistance to residents.
A licensed residential home in which the provider shares the home with a small number of adults and provides housing, meals and personal care.
Caregivers who are not agency employees but provide agency services under a written contract.
Communication with facility management and staff so that agency services, facility services and the resident's plan do not conflict or duplicate.

procedures: At referral, intake staff ask whether the client lives in an ALF or adult family care home, and record the facility name, address, administrator and phone number.

The RN supervisor reviews the request and, with the resident or representative, identifies what the facility already provides and what the agency would add. The agency does not accept a request that duplicates facility services.

The RN supervisor contacts the facility administrator or designee before the first visit to coordinate visit times, access, the resident's care plan, medication assistance arrangements, and how changes will be communicated. Contacts are recorded in the client record.

The agency confirms services can be provided safely and all assigned visits can be assured, including communication with the resident through a same-language staff person, interpreter or translation technology (Rule 59A-8.020(1); CR-06). The agency declines admission if it cannot.

An agency representative and the resident or the resident's representative sign and date a written agreement. A copy goes to the resident and the original goes in the file. For aide, homemaker and companion clients with no treatment order, the agreement is the service provision plan and is kept for one year after termination (Rule 59A-8.020(2)-(3); SVC-04, CR-07).
The agreement states that the agency is solely responsible for the services it provides, and states who is responsible for services the facility provides.
The RN supervisor develops the service plan to supplement, not replace, the facility's services, and shares the relevant portions with the facility with the resident's consent (CR-04).

Before the first visit, the RN supervisor obtains the facility's evacuation plan for the resident, records where the resident would go and who would be notified, and files this in the client record (SAF-07).

Caregivers sign in with the facility as required by facility policy. They follow facility visitor, infection control and security rules unless these conflict with agency policy or client rights, in which case they call the RN supervisor.
Caregivers report changes in the resident's condition to the RN supervisor, who notifies the facility and the resident's representative as appropriate (SVC-11).

If the facility interferes with agency services or the agency suspects neglect, the RN supervisor reports to the administrator the same day. The administrator contacts the facility, and staff report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation under SAF-01.
If the agency's office will be located in space within an ALF, the administrator sends AHCA written notice before operating there and keeps a copy in the compliance file (GOV-10).

The administrator keeps a current list of services provided directly by employees and services provided by contract, and checks that the license application and any changes match the list (Rule 59A-8.008(4)). Changes are reported under GOV-10.

Before any contracted caregiver works, the administrator confirms a written contract, current certification or training proof, Level 2 screening results and registry checks, and training records, and files them (PER-01 to PER-07).

The RN supervisor supervises contracted caregivers on the same schedule and under the same delegation rules as employees (SVC-05, SVC-06). The agency retains responsibility for the quality of contracted services.
The administrator reviews contracted services and facility coordination quarterly in QA (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Approves contracts, keeps the direct versus contract services list, gives AHCA required notices, and reviews facility coordination in QA.
Coordinates with the facility, develops the service plan, documents the evacuation plan and supervises employed and contracted caregivers.
Identifies facility residents at referral, checks safe-service and language needs, and prepares the written agreement.
Follow the service plan and facility rules, and report changes and concerns to the RN supervisor.

documentation: Facility coordination notes in the client record
Signed and dated service agreement and service provision plan
Facility evacuation plan for the resident
Contracts with contracted caregivers and credential files
List of services provided by employees versus contract
AHCA written notice if the agency's office is in an ALF
QA review of facility coordination

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All owners, administrators, managers, RN supervisors, home health aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions, contracted staff and volunteers
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation of clients and to make sure every suspected case is reported immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect or exploitation of any client. Any staff member who knows or suspects that a vulnerable adult has been abused, neglected or exploited must report it immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873. The duty to report belongs to each staff member individually and may not be delegated to or delayed by a supervisor. Reporting to the administrator does not replace the hotline report. The agency will post the hotline number in the office and give it to every client on or before the first day of service (s. 408.810(5), F.S.; CR-03). The agency screens owners, administrators, financial officers and direct-care staff at Level 2, rescreens every 5 years, and maintains screening through the Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse (ss. 408.809 and 435.12, F.S.; PER-03). Staff receive training on recognizing and reporting abuse at orientation and annually (Rule 59A-8.0095, F.A.C.; PER-04). The agency never retaliates against anyone who reports in good faith.

definitions.definition: A willful act or threatened act that causes or is likely to cause significant impairment to a vulnerable adult's physical, mental or emotional health.
Failure or omission by a caregiver to provide the care, supervision and services needed to maintain a client's physical and mental health.
Improper use of a client's funds, property or assets for another person's benefit.
The Department of Children and Families' statewide hotline, 1-800-962-2873.
Fingerprint-based state and national criminal history screening through the Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse.

procedures: At hire and before direct client contact, the administrator submits fingerprints for Level 2 screening through the AHCA Background Screening Unit and the Clearinghouse. No one may provide direct care until screening shows eligibility (PER-03).

The administrator tracks each person's 5-year rescreening date and keeps screening results in the personnel file. Rescreening is renewed through the Clearinghouse and is completed before the 5-year date (PER-07).

At orientation and every calendar year, the RN supervisor trains each staff member on the signs of abuse, neglect and exploitation, the duty to report, hotline procedures and non-retaliation. Training dates and sign-in sheets are filed (PER-04).
The administrator posts the Florida Abuse Hotline number (1-800-962-2873) in the office where staff and visitors can see it.
Intake staff give each client the hotline notices on or before the first day of service, record the date in the client record, and have the client or representative acknowledge receipt (CR-03).

Caregivers watch for warning signs during every visit: unexplained injuries, fear of a person, weight loss, poor hygiene, unpaid bills, missing belongings or money, changed wills or financial documents, and unsafe living conditions.

If a staff member knows or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member calls the Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately, from the client's home if safe or as soon as possible after leaving. The staff member records the date, time and name of the hotline intake worker.
If the client is in immediate danger or needs urgent medical care, the staff member first calls 911 and follows SVC-11, then reports to the hotline.

After reporting, the staff member notifies the RN supervisor and administrator the same day and completes an incident report as described in SAF-02. The administrator does not interview the client or alleged abuser in a way that interferes with the investigation.
The administrator cooperates fully with investigators from DCF, law enforcement and AHCA, and gives them access to records and staff as the law allows.

If the alleged perpetrator is a staff member, the administrator immediately removes that person from client contact and from all clients while the investigation is pending, and documents the action. The administrator reviews the person's personnel file and screening status.
If an allegation involves a client's property or money, staff follow CR-05 and the administrator secures related records.
The administrator keeps the hotline report confirmation number and incident report in the QA file, and reviews all allegations in QA (GOV-07).

The administrator protects the reporter's identity as far as possible and does not discipline, threaten, reassign or otherwise retaliate against any person who reports in good faith. Any report of retaliation is investigated immediately.
The RN supervisor and administrator review the service plan after any substantiated or suspected case and add protections as needed (SVC-04).

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the hotline immediately, then notify the RN supervisor and administrator.
Ensures screening, training and posting; removes accused staff from contact; cooperates with investigators; prevents retaliation.
Trains staff on recognition and reporting, assesses client safety and updates the service plan.
Gives hotline notices to clients on or before the first day of service.

documentation: Level 2 screening results and 5-year rescreening tracker
Training sign-in sheets and content for orientation and annual abuse training
Photo or description of the posted hotline notice
Client acknowledgment of hotline notices
Hotline report confirmation numbers
Incident reports and investigation notes
Actions taken, including removal of staff from client contact
QA review of allegations

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted staff, the RN supervisor, administrator and alternate administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident involving a client or staff member is reported, documented, reviewed and acted on promptly, and that QA uses incident data to prevent recurrence.
policies.policy: Staff report any incident, including a fall, injury, medication assistance error, property damage, or allegation of abuse, neglect or exploitation, to the RN supervisor and administrator the same day. The staff member completes a written incident report, which is filed in the client record and in the QA file. When abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected, staff also report to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 (SAF-01). Incident trends are reviewed quarterly in QA (GOV-07). Deaths and other events that AHCA requires the agency to report are reported through the channels set out in REC-03. Because the RN supervisor oversees aides and supervises medication assistance under Rule 59A-8.0095, F.A.C., the RN supervisor reviews every incident for needed changes to the service plan or caregiver training. The agency does not discipline staff for good-faith reporting of an incident.

definitions.definition: Any unplanned event that harms or could harm a client, staff member or visitor, or that damages property or involves an alleged violation of client rights.
A mistake made while helping a client self-administer medication, such as helping with the wrong medication, at the wrong time, or without the client's consent.
A written, dated and signed account of the facts of an incident, the response and the follow-up.
Quarterly QA analysis of incidents by type, caregiver, client, time and location.

procedures: The staff member first protects the client and, if needed, calls 911 and follows SVC-11. Reporting begins only after the client is safe.

The staff member telephones the RN supervisor and the administrator or alternate administrator on the same day as the incident, as soon as the client is safe, and states what happened, who was involved and what action was taken.
If abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected, the staff member calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately and follows SAF-01.

The staff member completes a written incident report the same day, or by the end of the next business day if the staff member is injured or unable to do so. The report states date, time, place, persons involved, witnesses, facts observed, injuries, action taken and who was notified. It uses factual, non-judgmental language.

The RN supervisor reviews the report within one business day. For client injuries, falls or medication assistance errors, the RN supervisor assesses the client (by visit or phone), notifies the client's physician or care provider if needed, and records the action.

The administrator or RN supervisor notifies the client's representative the same day when a client has been injured, a medication error has occurred, or the client has been involved in a serious incident (CR-04).
The administrator notifies the payer's care or support coordinator when required by the payer (SVC-13).
For medication assistance errors, the RN supervisor retrains the caregiver and re-observes the caregiver's competency before the caregiver resumes medication assistance (SVC-08).
The administrator files the original incident report in the client record and a copy in the QA incident file. Any internal memo about the incident is kept in the QA file, not in the client record.
The administrator decides whether the event is reportable to AHCA or another agency under REC-03, and if so, makes the report within the required time and records the date and confirmation.
The administrator logs every incident on the QA incident log the day the report is received, with the action taken and the date of closure.
Each quarter the QA committee reviews the log for trends by incident type, client, caregiver, time of day and location, and records corrective actions (GOV-07).
The administrator tracks corrective actions to completion and follows up within 30 days to verify they were effective.
The administrator reminds staff of this policy at orientation and annually in-service training (PER-04).

responsibilities.duty: Protect the client, report incidents to the RN supervisor and administrator the same day, and complete an incident report.
Reviews incidents, assesses clients, retrains caregivers, and updates the service plan.
Determines reportability, notifies required parties, maintains the incident log, and leads QA trend review.
Reviews incident trends quarterly and approves corrective actions.

documentation: Written incident reports in the client record
Copies of incident reports in the QA file
QA incident log
Notifications to representatives, physicians and payers
Hotline confirmation numbers
AHCA or other agency reports and confirmations
Quarterly QA minutes with trend findings and corrective actions

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted staff, the RN supervisor, administrator and anyone who enters a client's home on behalf of the agency
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among clients and staff by following recognized infection control practices during every visit.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(c)1, F.A.C. (official checklist item 59A-8.0095(2)(c)1, policies and procedures consistent with recommended CDC and OSHA guidelines for safety, universal precautions and infection control procedures). [AGENCY NAME]'s infection control practices are consistent with current recommended CDC and OSHA guidelines for safety, universal precautions and infection control procedures. Staff treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious and use standard (universal) precautions with every client. Basic infection control is a required topic of home health aide training (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c), topic 4; PER-02). The agency provides PPE at no cost to staff and, where staff have occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials, provides bloodborne pathogen training under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). Exposure incidents are documented and followed up.

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all clients, treating blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection.
Reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials while performing duties.
A specific contact with blood or other potentially infectious material that results from the performance of an employee's duties.

procedures: The administrator and RN supervisor review this policy against current CDC and OSHA guidance at least annually, and when either body issues new guidance that affects home care, and record the review (GOV-06).

The RN supervisor trains each new caregiver on infection control at orientation, covering hand hygiene, standard precautions, PPE, cleaning and disinfection, laundry, and handling of blood and body fluids, and verifies competency by return demonstration (PER-04).
For each client, the RN supervisor identifies infection risks during the assessment and tells caregivers what precautions are needed in the service plan (SVC-04).

Caregivers wash their hands with soap and water, or use alcohol-based hand rub when hands are not visibly soiled, at the start and end of each visit, before and after glove use, and before and after personal care, food handling and toileting assistance.

Caregivers wear gloves when contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, broken skin or soiled items is likely. They change gloves between tasks and between clients, and never reuse disposable gloves.
Caregivers use other PPE such as a gown, mask or eye protection when splashes or contact with respiratory secretions are likely. They remove and dispose of PPE before leaving the work area.
The agency supplies each caregiver with a PPE and hand hygiene kit and replaces supplies on request. Caregivers do not pay for PPE.
Caregivers clean and disinfect shared equipment and high-touch surfaces used in care, using EPA-registered disinfectants according to label directions.
Caregivers handle soiled linen and clothing without shaking and bag it at the point of use. Contaminated waste is handled under SAF-04.
Staff who have fever, diarrhea, vomiting, an infectious rash or respiratory symptoms notify the scheduling coordinator and RN supervisor and do not report for duty until cleared under PER-06.
The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccination series free of charge to staff with occupational exposure, as OSHA requires, and records acceptance or declination.

After any exposure incident, the staff member immediately washes the site with soap and water or flushes the mucous membrane, reports the exposure to the RN supervisor and administrator at once, and completes an incident report (SAF-02).
The RN supervisor arranges a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up for the exposed staff member as soon as possible, and records the actions taken.
The administrator logs exposure incidents and reviews them quarterly in QA to identify preventable causes and update training or supplies (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures PPE supply, hepatitis B vaccine offer, exposure follow-up and annual policy review.
Trains and checks caregiver competency, identifies infection risks for each client, and arranges exposure follow-up.
Follow standard precautions, use PPE, report exposures and illness, and handle waste and linen correctly.
Replaces staff who are ill and keeps PPE supplies available.

documentation: Annual policy review record with CDC and OSHA references
Orientation and in-service infection control training records
Bloodborne pathogen training records
Hepatitis B vaccine acceptance or declination forms
Exposure incident reports and medical follow-up records
PPE supply log
QA review of exposures

policies.title: Biomedical Waste and Sharps Handling
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted caregivers of [AGENCY NAME]; the Administrator, Alternate Administrator and supervising RN
policies.purpose: To protect clients, caregivers and the public from exposure to blood, body fluids, sharps and contaminated waste, and to have biomedical waste procedures in place before any skilled service is added.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed to provide non-skilled home health services only. We do not provide nursing or physical therapy services. Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(b), F.A.C. requires the director of nursing, administrator or alternate administrator to establish biomedical waste policies and procedures for agencies that provide nursing and physical therapy services. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(b), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.0095(2)(b) — Biomedical Waste). The requirement applies only if those services are provided. We adopt this policy now so it is in place if skilled services are added. Because we have no director of nursing, the Administrator, or the Alternate Administrator in the Administrator's absence, establishes and maintains these procedures. Home health aides and CNAs do not handle sharps or injectables (s. 400.488(4), F.S.). Caregivers do not dispose of a client's own sharps, such as lancets, insulin needles or syringes. If a caregiver finds or is exposed to a client's sharps, the caregiver does not touch them and notifies the RN supervisor. Contaminated disposable items from personal care are bagged and disposed of following CDC and OSHA guidance, including the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). If skilled services are added, this policy will be expanded under SVC-14 to cover sharps containers, labeling, storage, transport and a licensed biomedical waste disposal vendor under the state and local requirements in force at that time.

definitions.definition: Waste that is, or may be, contaminated with blood or other potentially infectious body fluids, including sharps and saturated or dripping soiled materials.
Needles, syringes, lancets and other items that can puncture or cut skin and may be contaminated with blood or body fluids.
A single-use item, such as a glove, incontinence brief, wipe or soiled dressing, that has contact with body fluids during personal care.
A needlestick, cut, splash or other contact of blood or other potentially infectious material with a caregiver's eyes, mouth, mucous membranes or broken skin.

procedures: The Administrator reviews this policy at each annual policy review (GOV-06) and before any skilled service, LPN or nursing task is added to the agency's scope (SVC-14).

At orientation (PER-04), the RN supervisor trains each caregiver on this policy and on standard precautions, including hand hygiene, gloves and when to change them. The caregiver signs and dates the training record.
The agency issues disposable gloves and other protective supplies at no cost to caregivers, and the RN supervisor shows each caregiver how to put them on and remove them safely.
Caregivers do not give injections, draw blood, perform finger-sticks or handle needles, syringes or lancets. This follows the aide scope in SVC-01.

If a caregiver sees a client's loose or used sharps, such as a needle on a table or floor, the caregiver does not pick them up, recap them or place them in the trash. The caregiver keeps others away, keeps the item in view if safe to do so, and calls the RN supervisor right away.

The RN supervisor tells the client or representative to use the client's own sharps container or a prescriber- or pharmacy-approved disposal method. The RN supervisor records this in the client record. Agency caregivers do not carry out the disposal.

Contaminated disposable items from personal care, such as soiled briefs, gloves and wipes, are placed in a sturdy plastic bag, sealed, and put in the client's regular household trash, following CDC and OSHA guidance. Items that are saturated or dripping with blood are not handled by the caregiver. The caregiver calls the RN supervisor for direction.
Reusable soiled linens and clothing are handled with gloves, kept away from the caregiver's body, and laundered per SAF-03. Caregivers do not shake or rinse soiled linens in a way that splashes.

If a caregiver has an exposure incident, the caregiver washes the area with soap and water or flushes the eyes or mucous membranes with water immediately. The caregiver then notifies the RN supervisor or Administrator on the same shift and seeks prompt medical evaluation.

The Administrator completes an incident report (SAF-02) and a workers' compensation first report of injury if applicable (SAF-08). The Administrator offers confidential follow-up as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 and keeps medical information separate from the personnel file (PER-07).
The RN supervisor reviews each exposure or sharps incident with the Administrator within 3 business days to find the cause and prevent a repeat. The review is documented in the QAPI records (GOV-07).

Before any skilled service is added, the Administrator drafts a written exposure control plan, selects a biomedical waste vendor, and updates this policy and the Procedure Manual. The Administrator documents the update date in the document control log (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Establishes and maintains this policy, makes sure training and supplies are in place, and updates the policy before skilled services are added. The Alternate Administrator acts in the Administrator's absence.
Trains caregivers, responds to sharps and exposure reports, and instructs clients on safe disposal of their own sharps.

responsibilities.role: Home health aides, CNAs and other caregivers
responsibilities.duty: Use standard precautions, do not handle sharps or injectables, bag contaminated disposables properly, and report sharps and exposures immediately.
Dispose of the client's own sharps by approved methods and tell the agency about sharps in the home.

documentation: Orientation and annual training records on standard precautions and sharps (PER-04)
Client record note when sharps are found and the RN supervisor is notified
Incident reports and exposure follow-up (confidential medical file)
QAPI review of sharps and exposure events
Document control log showing annual review of this policy

policies.title: Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan: Development, Approval, Annual Review and Contact Updates
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Alternate Administrator, RN Supervisor, scheduling staff and all employees designated for emergency duties
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has a written, state-approved, annually reviewed comprehensive emergency management plan (CEMP) and that county emergency officials always have working contact numbers for our emergency coordinators.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written CEMP prepared and maintained under s. 400.492, F.S. The plan follows the criteria and format of AHCA Form 3110-1022 (rev. 3/2013), and describes how the agency establishes and maintains an effective response to emergencies and disasters. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(1), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(1) — Written CEMP in AHCA Form 3110-1022 format). The completed plan is forwarded electronically to the contact designated by the Department of Health for approval, and the agency reviews the plan annually and makes substantive changes. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(2)-(3), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(2)-(3) — Electronic submission for approval; annual review). When the telephone numbers of staff who coordinate emergency response change, including after-hours numbers, the agency reports the change to the county Emergency Management office and the county health department. A new owner reviews the plan after a change of ownership. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(4)-(5), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(4)-(5) — Contact-number changes; review after change of ownership). A renewal license application needs a CEMP approval letter or proof of submission within the last 365 days, so the agency keeps the approval letter or submission proof current.

definitions.definition: The agency's Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan, written on AHCA Form 3110-1022 (rev. 3/2013) under s. 400.492, F.S.
A staff member named in the CEMP who coordinates the agency's emergency response and whose daytime and after-hours phone numbers are reported to county officials.
The emergency management agency of each county where the agency serves clients.
The Department of Health contact designated to receive and approve home health agency emergency plans electronically.

procedures: Before the license application is submitted, the Administrator names at least two emergency coordinators (a primary and a backup) and records their daytime and after-hours telephone numbers in the CEMP.

The Administrator completes the CEMP on AHCA Form 3110-1022 (rev. 3/2013), covering every section of the form. The plan reflects our non-skilled services, our service counties and the ALFs and adult family care homes we serve (SVC-15).

The Administrator sends the completed plan electronically to the Department of Health contact designated for plan approval. The Administrator saves the transmittal email or confirmation as proof of submission, with the date.
If the reviewer asks for changes, the Administrator revises the plan and resubmits it within 10 business days. This is an agency standard.

On receipt of the approval letter, the Administrator files the letter and the approved plan in the compliance binder. A paper copy of the plan is kept at [ADDRESS] and an electronic copy is stored where it can be reached off-site.

The Administrator reviews the plan once every 12 months and updates it to reflect any substantive changes. These include new counties served, a new client population, a changed vendor or facility partner, new staff roles and lessons learned from drills or actual events. The annual review is signed and dated by the Administrator and logged in GOV-06.

The Administrator resubmits the updated plan electronically after any substantive change and keeps proof of submission. At every license renewal, the Administrator confirms that the file holds a CEMP approval letter or proof of submission dated within the last 365 days, and attaches it to the renewal.

Whenever an emergency coordinator's telephone number changes, including an after-hours number, or a coordinator is replaced, the Administrator updates the CEMP and reports the change in writing to the county Emergency Management office and the county health department for every county served. This is done within 5 business days as an agency standard. The Administrator keeps the sent notices.
The Administrator verifies the coordinator contact list every quarter by calling each number, and documents the check.

After a change of ownership, the new owner or Administrator reviews the entire CEMP, updates owner and contact details, and documents the review with date and signature. This is coordinated with GOV-10.
At orientation and each year, the Administrator briefs all staff on the plan and on each person's role. Staff designated for emergency duties receive a copy of their duties (see SAF-06).
The Administrator holds at least one drill or tabletop exercise each year, records the results and uses them in the annual review and the QAPI program (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the CEMP, submits it for approval, completes the annual review, reports contact changes and keeps proof for license renewal.
Acts as the backup emergency coordinator and carries out these duties when the Administrator is unavailable.
Helps with clinical sections of the plan, including the prioritized client list and client emergency plans.
Know the plan, keep contact lists current and carry out assigned emergency duties.

responsibilities.role: New owner (after a change of ownership)
responsibilities.duty: Reviews and adopts the plan, as in GOV-10.

documentation: Current CEMP on AHCA Form 3110-1022 (rev. 3/2013)
Electronic submission confirmations and the Department of Health approval letter
Signed annual review record
Notices of emergency coordinator phone changes sent to the county Emergency Management office and county health department
Change-of-ownership plan review record
Drill and tabletop reports
Staff briefing and training sign-in sheets

policies.title: Emergency Staffing, Communication Contingency, Continuity of Care and Cessation of Operations
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Alternate Administrator, RN Supervisor, scheduling staff, caregivers designated for emergency duty
policies.purpose: To keep clients safe and supported during an emergency by assigning staff duties, keeping communication working when phones fail, contacting clients before a threat, defining how far we will continue care, and managing any cessation of operations.
policies.policy: In an emergency, [AGENCY NAME] informs all staff designated for emergency measures of their duties. If telephone service is unavailable, the agency uses a communication contingency plan, which may include cell phones, ham radio, public announcements, driving to the client's home, or contacting police or rescue services. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(6)(a)-(b), F.A.C. and s. 400.492, F.S. (official item 59A-8.027(6)(a)-(b) — Staff duties; communication contingency plan). On an imminent threat of an emergency, the agency contacts clients who need ongoing services, and the ALFs and adult family care homes it serves, to confirm each client's plan. Before an emergency, the agency establishes procedures stating how far it will continue care during and after the emergency. It finds out which clients who stay at home need agency care, and designates staff to continue services. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(9)-(10), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(9)-(10) — Contact on imminent threat; extent of continued care; designated staff). If the agency ceases operation during an emergency, it informs affected clients, notifies the ALFs and adult family care homes it serves, and arranges for essential services to continue. It reports its status to the local emergency operations center. When it cannot continue services to special needs clients, the record documents the efforts made to comply with the plan. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(11)-(12), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(11)-(12) — Cessation of operations; documentation of efforts).

definitions.definition: A hurricane watch or warning, flood warning, evacuation order or other official notice that an emergency is likely to affect the area where clients live.
Employees named in the CEMP who have assigned duties during an emergency, such as coordinating, calling clients or staffing visits.
Backup ways to reach clients, staff and officials when regular telephone service is out.
Services a client cannot safely go without, such as help with eating, toileting, transfers or personal hygiene, as listed in the client's service plan.

procedures: In the CEMP, the Administrator assigns each emergency duty (command, client calls, staff calls, scheduling, record access, supplies, liaison with county officials) to a named person and a backup.
Each year, and whenever duties change, the Administrator gives every designated staff member a written statement of their duties and records the briefing with date and signature.

The Administrator keeps and updates a communication contingency plan listing at least three ways to reach clients and staff if phones are down. Options include cell phones and text messaging, ham radio operators, public announcements, driving to the client's home, and contacting police or rescue services. The plan lists the phone number of the county Emergency Management office.
Before the start of each hurricane season and whenever the plan changes, the Administrator tests the backup communication methods and records the results.
When an imminent threat is announced, the Administrator or Alternate Administrator activates the CEMP and notes the date and time in the emergency log.

Within 24 hours of activation, or sooner if the threat is closer, the designated staff call each client who needs ongoing services, starting with the prioritized client list (SAF-07). They confirm whether the client is evacuating or staying, where the client will be, and how to reach the client. They also confirm whether a caregiver can take over care.

Designated staff call each ALF and adult family care home where the agency serves residents, and confirm the facility's plan for the residents we serve (SVC-15). The facility's response is documented in the client record.

The Administrator and RN supervisor decide, and record in the CEMP before any emergency, how far the agency will continue care during and after an emergency (for example, which visits continue until conditions become unsafe and which resume first afterward). The decision considers staff safety and official orders.

For each client staying at home who needs agency care, the RN supervisor identifies the essential services in the service plan and assigns a named caregiver. The caregiver is told the visit plan and how to reach the agency.

After the emergency, the designated staff contact each client who needed ongoing services as soon as conditions allow, starting with special needs clients. They check on the client's safety and resume or adjust services. Each contact is documented.

If the agency cannot continue operating, the Administrator personally or through designees informs every affected client or representative, using the communication contingency methods if needed. The Administrator notifies each ALF and adult family care home served, and arranges for essential services to continue through another provider, the family or facility staff, and the payer where applicable (SVC-13).
The Administrator reports the agency's status to the local emergency operations center for each county affected.

When the agency cannot continue services to a special needs client, the RN supervisor or Administrator documents in that client's record each effort made to comply with the plan, including the date, time, person contacted and result.
Within 30 days after any activation, the Administrator holds a review with staff of what worked and what did not, updates the CEMP (SAF-05) and records the findings in QAPI (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Activates the plan, assigns duties, ensures client and facility contact, reports status to the emergency operations center and leads any cessation notices.
Acts for the Administrator and serves as backup emergency coordinator.
Identifies essential services, assigns caregivers for clients staying at home and documents efforts for special needs clients.
Make assigned calls, carry out assigned visits, and document contacts and visits.

documentation: Written emergency duty assignments and signed staff briefing records
Communication contingency plan and test results
Emergency activation log
Client and facility contact records
Records of services provided or not provided during the emergency, including documented efforts for special needs clients
Notices to clients, facilities and the local emergency operations center
After-action review report

policies.title: Client Emergency Preparedness at Admission, Special Needs Registry and In-Home Medication Lists
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, RN Supervisor, Administrator, Alternate Administrator and all staff who admit or serve clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every client has an emergency plan on record from admission, that clients needing continuing care are registered with the county special needs registry, and that emergency information and medication lists are available at the client's home and to county officials.
policies.policy: At admission, [AGENCY NAME] informs each client and caregiver about the county special needs registry (s. 252.355, F.S.). The agency documents in the client file whether the client will evacuate or stay, whether the caregiver can take over services, and whether the agency must continue services. For an ALF or adult family care home resident, the agency finds out the facility's evacuation plan and documents it. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(8), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(8) — Admission notice of the special needs registry and evacuation plan). The agency collects registration information for special needs clients who need continuing care in a disaster and submits it to the county Emergency Management office. It educates registered clients that special needs shelters are an option of last resort and that services there may not equal those received at home. This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(13)-(14), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(13)-(14) — Special needs registration and shelter education). The agency maintains a current prioritized client list with the information required by s. 400.492(2), F.S., and furnishes it to the county health department and Emergency Management office on request. Each special needs client's record includes the information required by s. 400.492(1), F.S. The agency keeps in the special needs client's home a list of client-specific medications, supplies and equipment (names, dose, frequency, route, time, allergies, physician, pharmacy). This policy meets Rule 59A-8.027(15)-(17), F.A.C. (official item 59A-8.027(15)-(17) — Prioritized client list; special needs client record; in-home medication, supply and equipment list). We provide only non-skilled care. The medication list is a record of what the client takes, for emergency responders. Caregivers do not manage or change medications (SVC-08).

definitions.definition: The county registry established under s. 252.355, F.S., for persons who need assistance or sheltering in a disaster.
A client who needs continuing care in a disaster and for whom registration information is collected and sent to county Emergency Management.
A current list that ranks clients by need for continued service in an emergency and includes the information required by s. 400.492(2), F.S.

definitions.term: In-home medication, supply and equipment list
definitions.definition: A list kept in the client's home that gives medication names, dose, frequency, route and time, along with allergies, physician, pharmacy and the client's supplies and equipment.

procedures: During the admission assessment (SVC-03), intake staff or the RN supervisor explains the county special needs registry to the client and caregiver and gives them the registration contact information for their county. Staff record the date this was done.

At the same visit, staff complete the emergency preparedness section of the client record. They document whether the client will evacuate or stay, where the client would go, whether a caregiver can take over services, and whether the agency must continue services.
For a client living in an ALF or adult family care home, staff ask for the facility's evacuation plan, record it in the client file, and ask for an updated plan each year (SVC-15).

The RN supervisor identifies each client who would need continuing care in a disaster and who is a special needs client. With the client's consent, the RN supervisor collects the registration information required by the county.

The Administrator submits the registration information for special needs clients to the county Emergency Management office. The submission date and county are recorded in the client file. Where the client or caregiver must complete the registry application personally, staff help and follow up.

Staff tell each registered client that special needs shelters are an option of last resort and that services at a shelter may not equal those received at home. The client's understanding is documented.

The Administrator keeps a prioritized client list that is updated when a client is admitted, discharged or has a change in condition, and in any case reviewed at least quarterly. The list includes the information required by s. 400.492(2), F.S.
On request, the Administrator furnishes the current prioritized client list to the county health department and the county Emergency Management office, and records the date and requester.
The record of each special needs client includes the information required by s. 400.492(1), F.S. The RN supervisor checks each special needs record for completeness at admission and every 6 months.

For each special needs client, the RN supervisor obtains the medication, supply and equipment information from the client's current medication list and the client or caregiver, and writes a list that includes name, dose, frequency, route, time, allergies, physician and pharmacy.
The list is placed in the client's home in a spot agreed on with the client, and the client or caregiver is told where it is. Caregivers confirm at visits that the list is present.

When a medication, supply or equipment item changes, the RN supervisor updates the home list within 2 business days as an agency standard. The caregiver reports changes seen at the home to the RN supervisor.

Before each hurricane season, the RN supervisor reviews every special needs client's emergency plan and home list with the client or caregiver and documents the review. Clients who need follow-up are called under SAF-06 when a threat is imminent.
Clients who decline registration or an emergency plan are told of the risks. The refusal is documented and signed where possible, and the client may change the decision at any time.

responsibilities.duty: Explain the special needs registry at admission and record the client's evacuation or stay decision.
Identifies special needs clients, collects registration data, builds the in-home lists and checks record completeness.
Submits registration information to the county, maintains the prioritized client list and responds to county requests.
Check that the in-home list is present and report changes in medications, supplies or equipment to the RN supervisor.

documentation: Emergency preparedness section of the admission record, with registry notice date
Special needs registration submissions to county Emergency Management
Prioritized client list with update dates
Records of lists furnished to the county health department or Emergency Management office
In-home medication, supply and equipment lists and update dates
ALF or adult family care home evacuation plans
Documentation of client shelter education and any refusal

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted caregivers, the RN Supervisor, the Administrator and Alternate Administrator
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from injury, exposure and violence while working in clients' homes and to set out when they may leave, whom to call and how events are documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] works to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards, consistent with the OSHA General Duty Clause (29 U.S.C. 654), and follows the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) for exposure to blood and body fluids. Caregivers are trained to maintain a clean and safe environment and to use safe transfer techniques (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c), F.A.C.). Any caregiver may leave an unsafe home. Unsafe conditions include threats, violence, sexual harassment, weapons displayed in a threatening way, impaired persons, hazardous conditions and fire, gas or structural dangers. The caregiver then calls the RN supervisor or Administrator and documents the event. The agency provides an after-hours contact so caregivers can reach a supervisor whenever clients are being served. No caregiver is penalized for leaving in good faith or for reporting a safety concern. The agency carries workers' compensation insurance. Coverage is mandatory for a non-construction employer with four or more employees, counting part-time employees (s. 440.02, F.S.). Where a client's behavior contributes to the danger, the RN supervisor reassesses the service plan (SVC-04) and the Administrator decides whether services can safely continue (SVC-12).

definitions.definition: Any threat, physical attack, harassment, intimidation or other disruptive behavior directed at a caregiver, including by a client, family member or visitor.
A client's home where the caregiver reasonably believes there is a risk of serious harm from violence, threats, hazards, impairment or conditions such as fire, gas leak or structural damage.
The telephone number of a supervisor who answers calls during all hours when caregivers are on duty.
Infection control practices that treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, such as gloves and hand hygiene.

procedures: During the admission assessment (SVC-03), the RN supervisor screens the home and household for safety risks. These include weapons, aggressive behavior, pets, smoking and oxygen, clutter and trip hazards, pests, lighting and the neighborhood. The findings are recorded and shared with the assigned caregiver.

At orientation (PER-04) and each year, the RN supervisor trains every caregiver on home safety, safe transfers and body mechanics, preventing falls, standard precautions, fire safety and how to de-escalate and leave a violent situation.

The service plan lists any safety precautions needed (for example, a second caregiver, mechanical lift use is not performed unless trained, pet restrained during visits). Assigned caregivers review the plan before the first visit.

Each caregiver has the telephone number of the after-hours contact, and the number is on the caregiver's ID or schedule. The Administrator makes sure a supervisor answers this line whenever clients are being served.

If a caregiver feels unsafe on arrival or during a visit, the caregiver may leave the home immediately. If it is safe to do so, the caregiver tells the client or others present that they are leaving, and calls the RN supervisor or after-hours contact.

If there is immediate danger, the caregiver calls 911 first, then the agency. The caregiver does not stay to argue, restrain a client or confront anyone, and does not remain in a home with a threatening person.

If the client cannot be left alone safely, the caregiver tells the RN supervisor, who arranges for a family member, another caregiver or emergency help. Leaving the home does not end the agency's duty to arrange for the client's safety under SVC-11.

The supervisor documents the event the same day. The caregiver completes an incident report (SAF-02) before the end of the shift or by the next business day if injured, describing what happened in factual terms.
If an event involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of the client, the supervisor reports it under SAF-01, including to the Florida Abuse Hotline (1-800-962-2873).

If a caregiver is hurt, the caregiver reports the injury to the Administrator the same day, receives medical care and the Administrator files the workers' compensation first report of injury. The agency keeps required workers' compensation coverage in force and checks coverage status once a year, and whenever the number of employees changes, to confirm that it is still required.
After an exposure to blood or body fluids, the caregiver follows SAF-04 and 29 CFR 1910.1030, including prompt medical evaluation.

Within 3 business days of a safety event, the RN supervisor and Administrator meet with the caregiver to offer support and decide what must change. They may add a second caregiver, change the schedule or set behavior expectations with the client or family. The outcome is recorded.
The Administrator reviews all safety incidents and workers' compensation claims at least quarterly in the QAPI program (GOV-07) to find trends and make changes.
The agency does not retaliate against any caregiver who reports a hazard, refuses unsafe work in good faith, or reports workplace violence.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains workers' compensation coverage, ensures an after-hours contact, reviews incidents and corrects hazards.
Screens homes for safety, trains caregivers, responds to calls, and adjusts service plans for safety.
Follow safe work practices, leave unsafe homes, call the supervisor, and document and report events.
Fills the Administrator's responsibilities in the Administrator's absence.

documentation: Home safety screening in the client record
Safety training records at orientation and annually (PER-04)
Incident reports and supervisor follow-up notes (SAF-02)
Workers' compensation policy and first reports of injury
After-hours contact schedule
QAPI quarterly review of safety events

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted caregivers who may drive clients, the RN Supervisor, the Administrator and scheduling staff
policies.purpose: To control the risks of transporting clients so that it is done only when authorized, by qualified and insured drivers, with proper restraints and with fair reimbursement of work travel.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] transports clients only when transport is authorized in writing in the client's service agreement (CR-07) and the driver is licensed and insured. Before authorizing any driver, the agency checks hired and non-owned auto coverage and confirms the driver's license and driving record. Drivers use child and mobility safety restraints as applicable. Work travel is reimbursed at the IRS standard mileage rate (72.5 cents per mile for 2026) unless the agency's own written plan states a different rate. Employees injured while driving on agency business are covered by workers' compensation where the agency is required to carry it (s. 440.02, F.S.; SAF-08). Transport is not part of the home health aide scope unless the service agreement and the service plan include it. Homemaker and companion staff may drive clients only under the same conditions (SVC-02).

definitions.definition: Liability insurance for vehicles the agency does not own, including employees' personal vehicles used on agency business.
An employee or contractor approved in writing by the Administrator to drive clients after license, record and insurance checks.
A seat belt, child restraint seat or wheelchair tie-down and occupant restraint appropriate to the passenger.
Travel for agency business, such as driving a client to an appointment or running a client errand, not the employee's regular commute.

procedures: Transport is considered at intake (SVC-03). If the client wants it, the Administrator and RN supervisor decide whether the agency can provide it safely, based on the client's ability to sit and transfer, mobility equipment and the assigned caregiver's training.

If transport is approved, it is written into the service agreement (CR-07), signed by the client or representative, with the purposes, destinations and any fees. Without written authorization, caregivers do not transport clients, except in an emergency when 911 is called instead.

Before authorizing a driver, the Administrator obtains a copy of a valid driver's license and runs a driving record check. The Administrator decides under written criteria whether the record is acceptable. The driver's license is rechecked once a year.

The Administrator confirms that the agency's hired and non-owned auto coverage applies to the vehicle and the driver. If the caregiver uses a personal vehicle, the caregiver gives proof of current personal auto insurance and the agency confirms how that coverage and agency coverage work together. The Administrator keeps the proof in the file.
The Administrator places authorized drivers on a list kept by scheduling staff. Scheduling staff assign transport visits only to drivers on the list.

Before driving, the driver checks that the vehicle is in safe working order and that all passengers are properly restrained. Children are placed in an appropriate child restraint seat. Clients who use wheelchairs are transported only in a vehicle fitted with a tie-down system and by a driver trained to use it. Otherwise the client transfers to a vehicle seat only if the client can do so safely under the service plan.
Drivers do not use handheld phones, drive when impaired or drowsy, carry more people than there are seats and restraints, or leave a client unattended in a vehicle.

Drivers help the client in and out of the vehicle only in ways they were trained for under the safe transfer techniques in the service plan. They do not lift a client beyond their training or the plan.

If a client's condition changes during a trip, the driver finds a safe place to stop, calls 911 if the situation is an emergency, and then calls the RN supervisor (SVC-11). If a crash occurs, the driver calls 911 and then the agency.
The driver completes a trip log with date, client, start and end odometer or mileage, and destinations. The log is turned in with the timesheet.

Mileage for work travel is reimbursed at the IRS standard rate, 72.5 cents per mile for 2026, unless the agency's own written mileage plan sets a different rate. The agency updates the rate each January. Time spent driving a client on agency business is paid work time (PER-08).

Any crash, injury or near miss is reported to the Administrator the same day and documented as an incident (SAF-02). The Administrator notifies the insurer and files a workers' compensation report if an employee is hurt.
The Administrator reviews transport incidents, authorized driver records and insurance coverage each year in the QAPI program (GOV-07) and removes any driver who no longer meets the criteria.

responsibilities.duty: Approves transport, checks insurance coverage and driver records, authorizes drivers and approves the mileage plan.
Assesses whether transport is safe for each client and sets any transfer or restraint instructions in the service plan.
Assign transport only to authorized drivers and collect trip logs.
Drive safely, use restraints, keep trip logs and report incidents.

documentation: Service agreement showing written transport authorization (CR-07)
Driver's license copy and driving record review
Proof of auto insurance and hired and non-owned auto coverage
List of authorized drivers
Trip logs and mileage reimbursement records
Incident reports for transport events (SAF-02)
Annual review of driver status and coverage

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications, Registry and Certification (CNAs and Home Health Aides)
policies.applies_to: Non-skilled Home Health Agency license: all certified nursing assistants (CNAs) and home health aides who provide hands-on personal care
policies.purpose: To make sure that only qualified, documented CNAs and home health aides give hands-on personal care to [AGENCY NAME] clients, and that the proof of qualification is in the file before the first client visit.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assigns hands-on personal care (bathing, dressing, eating, hygiene, transfers) only to CNAs and home health aides who meet this policy. Companions and homemakers may not provide hands-on personal care (s. 400.462, F.S.). This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(b)-(c), F.A.C. Under (5)(b), before a CNA works, the personnel file must contain current Florida CNA certification or a copy of another state's current certificate. Under (5)(c), before a home health aide works, the personnel file must contain documentation of at least 40 hours of training or a passed competency test. The training or test documentation must be in the file before the aide serves any client. No one is scheduled for hands-on care until the RN Supervisor or Administrator has verified the file and signed the qualification checklist. The 40-hour training must cover these 16 subjects: (1) communication skills; (2) observation, reporting and documentation; (3) reading and recording temperature, pulse and respiration; (4) basic infection control; (5) basic body functions to be reported to the RN supervisor; (6) maintenance of a clean and safe environment; (7) recognition of emergencies and follow-up; (8) physical, emotional and developmental characteristics of the populations served, including respect for the client, privacy and property; (9) personal hygiene and grooming techniques; (10) safe transfer techniques and ambulation; (11) normal range of motion and positioning; (12) nutrition and fluid intake; (13) cultural differences in families; (14) food preparation and household chores; (15) assistance with self-administered medication (a minimum of 2 hours, including verification that the aide can read the prescription label); and (16) other pertinent topics.

definitions.definition: A certified nursing assistant who holds current Florida certification, or a current certificate from another state, as documented in the personnel file.
A person who provides hands-on personal care under the supervision of an RN and who has documented 40 hours of training or a passed competency test.
Direct physical help with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, eating, hygiene and transfers. Companions and homemakers may not provide it.
The Home Health Aide Competency Test, AHCA 3110-1007, described in PER-02.

procedures: The Administrator or designee advertises caregiver openings by role and states in the posting whether the position involves hands-on care (CNA/home health aide) or companion/homemaker duties only.

At the application stage, the personnel designee asks each applicant to state whether he or she holds Florida CNA certification, an out-of-state CNA certificate, 40-hour aide training or a passed competency test.

For a Florida CNA, the personnel designee verifies certification before the first client visit by primary-source lookup through the Florida Board of Nursing's online license verification. The designee prints or saves the result with the date and the verifier's initials.
For a CNA certified in another state, the personnel designee obtains a copy of the current certificate and files it. The designee confirms that the certificate is current and not expired.

For an applicant without CNA certification who will work as a home health aide, the personnel designee obtains a certificate or transcript showing at least 40 hours of training that covers all 16 subjects listed in this policy. Alternatively, the designee obtains the signed passing result of the Home Health Aide Competency Test (AHCA 3110-1007).

If the applicant's training certificate does not show all 16 subjects, the RN Supervisor reviews it. If any subject or the 2-hour medication-assistance component is missing, the applicant completes the missing content under PER-02 before being scheduled, or the applicant takes the competency test.

The RN Supervisor confirms that the training record shows the 2 hours of self-administered medication assistance, including a check that the aide can read a prescription label, as required by Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)15, and records the check. Aides do not assist with medications until this is documented (see SVC-08 and PER-04).

The personnel designee completes the Caregiver Qualification Checklist (certification or training/test evidence, date verified, verifier). The RN Supervisor or Administrator signs and dates it before the first client visit.
The scheduler may assign a caregiver to hands-on care only when the qualification checklist is signed. The scheduler checks the checklist, not the caregiver's statement, before the first assignment.

Staff who hold no CNA certification and no aide training or passed test may be hired only as companions or homemakers, and only after the registration and training requirements in GOV-04, SVC-02 and PER-03 are met. They are never assigned hands-on care.

The personnel designee tracks the expiration date of each Florida CNA certification and each out-of-state certificate. The designee re-verifies certification before it lapses. A caregiver whose certification lapses is removed from CNA assignments until the file shows current certification.

If a caregiver is found to have been assigned without complete qualification documentation, the Administrator removes the caregiver from hands-on care the same day. The RN Supervisor reviews the visits already made, and the Administrator records the event and the corrective action in the QA log (GOV-07).

The Administrator reviews a sample of personnel files each quarter to confirm that qualification documents were in place before each caregiver's first visit. Results are reported to the governing body under GOV-07.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure no caregiver gives hands-on care before the qualification checklist is complete. Handles exceptions and corrective action.
Reviews training content against the 16 subjects. Verifies the medication-assistance component. Signs the qualification checklist.
Runs certification verification, collects and files documents, and tracks expiration dates.
Assigns hands-on visits only to caregivers whose checklist is signed.

documentation: Caregiver Qualification Checklist signed and dated before the first visit
Dated Florida CNA certification verification printout, or copy of the current out-of-state certificate
40-hour training certificate showing the 16 subjects and the 2-hour medication-assistance component, or the competency test result (AHCA 3110-1007) with the passing score
Certification expiration tracking log
Quarterly personnel file audit results

policies.title: Home Health Aide Training Program, Competency Testing and Instructor Qualifications
policies.applies_to: Non-skilled Home Health Agency license: any home health aide who is trained or tested by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] trains or tests home health aides, who may teach and evaluate them, and what proof is kept.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(h)-(i), F.A.C. Under (5)(h), any home health aide training [AGENCY NAME] provides is performed by, or under the general supervision of, an RN with at least 2 years of nursing experience, at least one of them in home health care. Under (5)(i), the agency may instead administer the Home Health Aide Competency Test (AHCA 3110-1007) and must keep documentation of the aide's passing result. The test requires the aide to perform all 14 practical tasks and to answer at least 90 of the 104 written questions correctly. An RN, or an LPN under RN supervision, administers and evaluates the practical portion. Training and testing may be delivered in person, online or in a hybrid format, but the aide must demonstrate skills in person. Any aide training course taught by the agency also follows the limits in Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(f)-(h), and the course must cover the 16 subjects in PER-01. The aide's file must show the completed training or passing result before the aide serves any client.

definitions.definition: Supervision by an RN who plans and oversees the course content and instructors and is available to them, without being present for every session.
A Florida-licensed RN with at least 2 years of nursing experience, one of them in home health care, documented in the RN's personnel file.
The Home Health Aide Competency Test form (September 2025 version): 14 practical tasks and 104 written questions.
The in-person demonstration of the 14 required tasks, evaluated by an RN or by an LPN under RN supervision.

procedures: The Administrator decides in writing whether the agency will (a) provide aide training, (b) use the competency test, or (c) accept only outside training and testing documentation under PER-01. The decision and date are recorded in the policy file.

The Administrator designates a qualified instructor RN, [INSTRUCTOR RN NAME]. The personnel designee checks and files proof of the RN's current Florida license, a resume or employment history showing at least 2 years of nursing experience, and the specific year(s) of home health experience.

If an LPN will evaluate the practical portion, the Administrator documents the LPN's current Florida license and the name of the supervising RN. The LPN's role is limited to administering and evaluating the test under the RN's supervision. It does not authorize skilled services (see SVC-14).

If the agency teaches aide training, the instructor RN writes a course outline covering all 16 subjects in PER-01, with hours per subject and at least 2 hours on assistance with self-administered medication, including label reading. The Administrator approves the outline. The outline is reviewed against Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(f)-(h) before the first class and whenever the rule is amended.

Course sessions may be in person, online or hybrid. For each aide, the instructor RN schedules an in-person skills demonstration and does not sign off the course until the aide has demonstrated the skills in person.
If the agency uses the competency test, the instructor RN uses the current AHCA 3110-1007 form. Before each test, the RN confirms with AHCA's posted forms that the version in use is current.
The RN (or LPN under RN supervision) observes each aide perform all 14 practical tasks and scores each task on the form. An aide who misses any practical task has not passed.
The aide takes the 104-question written test. A score of at least 90 correct answers is required to pass. The scorer records the score on the form.
The evaluating RN or LPN signs and dates the completed test form. The RN Supervisor reviews it and confirms that the aide has passed all 14 practical tasks and the written portion.

An aide who does not pass is not assigned to any client for hands-on care. The aide may be retrained by the instructor RN and retested. Each attempt is documented with the date, the tasks or sections missed and the instructor's remediation notes.

The personnel designee places the training certificate or the passed test form in the aide's personnel file (PER-07) and notes the date on the PER-01 qualification checklist. The aide is not scheduled until this is done.

For outside training, the personnel designee requests the course outline and hours from the provider. The RN Supervisor confirms that the content matches the required subjects before accepting the certificate.

Each year the Administrator reviews the training or testing program, including instructor credentials, current test form, delivery method and pass rates, and records the review in the QA minutes (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Decides which approach the agency uses. Approves the course outline. Makes sure the instructor meets the RN qualifications.
Teaches or supervises the course, administers and evaluates the practical portion, and signs the results.
Reviews outside training and completed test forms. Confirms eligibility before the aide is scheduled.
Keeps instructor credentials and aide test or training records in the correct files.

documentation: Instructor RN license, resume and experience verification (2 years' nursing, one in home health)
LPN license and supervising RN designation, if an LPN evaluates the practical portion
Course outline with hours and subjects, and attendance rosters (if the agency teaches)
