Completed Home Health Aide Competency Test, AHCA 3110-1007, with scores and signature of the evaluator
Remediation and retest records
Record of the in-person skills demonstration for each aide
Annual program review in QA minutes

policies.title: Background Checks and Employee Registries
policies.applies_to: Non-skilled Home Health Agency license and Homemaker and Companion Services registration: owners, administrator, financial officer and all client-contact staff
policies.purpose: To keep people with disqualifying offenses away from clients, to make sure Level 2 screening is completed and renewed, and to verify each worker's employment history.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires Level 2 fingerprint background screening through the Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse for owners, the administrator, the financial officer and every employee who has client contact, before any client contact (ss. 408.809 and 435.12, F.S.). Screening is rescreened every 5 years through the Clearinghouse. The agency also verifies each worker's employment history, with two documented attempts (diligent effort) to verify it (s. 400.509(4), F.S.; Rule 59A-8.025(7), F.A.C.). The agency does not assign anyone with a disqualifying offense to client contact and checks the Clearinghouse for results. Staff who work under the homemaker and companion registration are screened and verified in the same way.

definitions.definition: Fingerprint-based state and national criminal history screening, with results shared through the Clearinghouse.
The Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse, which shares fingerprint results among agencies and is used to renew screening (s. 435.12, F.S.).
Two documented attempts to verify a worker's employment or contractual history (Rule 59A-8.025(7), F.A.C.).
An offense that prohibits employment in a position of client contact under s. 408.809, F.S., unless an exemption has been granted.

procedures: The Administrator identifies every person who must be screened: each owner, the administrator, the alternate administrator, the financial officer and all employees with client contact, including CNAs, aides, homemakers and companions. The list is kept current in the screening tracking log.

Before the first day of work, the personnel designee gives each person the agency's screening instructions and arranges for electronic fingerprints at an approved vendor. The agency's Clearinghouse registration and number are given to the vendor when the agency's profile is established.

The personnel designee enters or links the person to the agency in the Clearinghouse. If a current screening already exists, the designee checks the Clearinghouse and records the result. The designee does not rely on the applicant's statement.

The personnel designee checks the Clearinghouse for results. If results are not yet available, the person has no client contact and is not scheduled for any client visit. Only the Clearinghouse result, not an applicant's statement or a private background check, is accepted as proof.

If the Clearinghouse shows an eligible result, the designee prints or saves it with the date and places it in the personnel file (PER-07). The designee records the date in the tracking log and the date the 5-year rescreen is due.

If the result shows a disqualifying offense or is ineligible, the Administrator removes the person from consideration or, for current staff, from all client contact on the same day. The Administrator documents the action. The agency does not pay or schedule the person for any client contact. If the person claims an exemption, the agency follows the exemption process under s. 408.809, F.S., and does not allow client contact until the exemption is granted.
For clearinghouse questions, the personnel designee calls the AHCA Background Screening Unit at 850-412-4503 or emails bgscreen@ahca.myflorida.com.

For every worker, the personnel designee contacts previous employers or contracting parties to verify employment or contractual history. The first attempt is made before the worker's first client visit. If there is no response, the designee makes a second attempt on a different day.

The designee records each attempt: date, time, method (phone, email, mail), name of the person contacted, and result. Two documented attempts are the minimum for diligent effort. If a second attempt does not produce a response, the designee notes that in the file and the Administrator initials it.

If verification reveals a discrepancy (for example, an undisclosed employer, a termination for abuse or exploitation, or falsified dates), the Administrator reviews it before the worker is assigned and may decline to employ the worker.

At least 120 days before each worker's 5-year screening anniversary, the personnel designee starts the Clearinghouse rescreening process, using the tracking log. The Administrator is notified of anyone not completed 30 days before the due date. Anyone whose rescreen lapses is removed from client contact until a current eligible result is in the Clearinghouse.

The personnel designee reconciles the Clearinghouse employee list with the current staff roster every month. People who have left the agency are removed from the agency's Clearinghouse profile, and new staff are added.
Screening records are kept in the personnel file and are accessible only to the Administrator and the personnel designee.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on any disqualifying result. Makes sure no one has client contact before an eligible result is on file.
Arranges fingerprinting, checks the Clearinghouse, performs employment verification and maintains the tracking log and rescreen dates.
Does not assign any staff member who is not shown as cleared in the tracking log.

documentation: Clearinghouse eligibility result for each person, with the date checked
Screening tracking log with the 5-year rescreen due dates
Employment history verification log showing two documented attempts for each worker
Records of any removal from client contact and any exemption request
Monthly Clearinghouse roster reconciliation

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual In-Service Training
policies.applies_to: Non-skilled Home Health Agency license: all home health aides and CNAs; orientation applies to all staff, including homemakers and companions
policies.purpose: To make sure every caregiver is oriented before serving clients, is evaluated as competent, receives in-service training each calendar year and holds current CPR.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(k), F.A.C.: home health aides and CNAs receive in-service training each calendar year and maintain current CPR certification from an approved provider, such as the American Red Cross or the American Heart Association. In addition, each employee completes orientation before the first client visit. Orientation covers agency policies, abuse reporting, infection control, emergency procedures and client rights. Before an aide assists any client with medication, the aide completes the 2-hour medication-assistance training required by Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)15, including the label-reading check. Attendance, topics and hours are documented for every employee. Dementia and HIV/AIDS training are completed on the schedules in PER-05.

definitions.definition: Training given to new staff before the first client visit on the agency's policies and the basic safety and rights topics listed in this policy.
Continuing education given to aides and CNAs each calendar year.
An organization such as the American Red Cross or the American Heart Association whose card or certificate shows an expiration date.
An RN's documented observation of an aide performing the tasks on the service plan, confirming that the aide can do them safely.

procedures: After the PER-01 qualification checklist and PER-03 screening are complete, the RN Supervisor or the Administrator schedules the new employee's orientation before the first client visit.

Orientation covers at least: agency policies and procedures; abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting, including the Florida Abuse Hotline 1-800-962-2873 (SAF-01); infection control (SAF-03); emergency procedures and the agency's emergency plan (SAF-05 to SAF-07); client rights (CR-01); privacy and confidentiality (CR-04); staff conduct (PER-09); documentation and electronic visit verification (SVC-10); and what to do when a client's condition changes (SVC-11).
The trainer records the orientation date, topics, hours and trainer name on the orientation record. The employee signs it. The record is filed in the personnel file.

The RN Supervisor evaluates the competency of each new aide and CNA by direct observation, in person, performing the personal care tasks they will be assigned, before or at the first assignment. The RN documents the tasks observed, the date and the result.
If the RN finds a skill gap, the aide receives additional instruction and is observed again. The aide is not assigned independently to that task until competency is documented.

Before any aide assists with self-administered medication, the RN Supervisor confirms and documents that the aide has completed the 2-hour medication-assistance training and demonstrated the ability to read a prescription label (SVC-08).

Each aide and CNA must hold current CPR certification from an approved provider such as the American Red Cross or the American Heart Association. The personnel designee obtains a copy of the card before the first visit, records the expiration date in the training tracker, and files the card.
The personnel designee sends reminders to each employee 60 days before CPR expires. An aide whose CPR lapses is not scheduled for client visits until a new certificate is on file.

The RN Supervisor prepares an annual in-service calendar each January. Topics include those required by rule and agency policy and those identified through QA findings, incident trends and client changes (GOV-07, SAF-02).
Each aide and CNA completes in-service training in each calendar year. The RN Supervisor checks the hours against the amount required by Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(k) and agency policy.

For every session, the trainer records the date, topic, hours, trainer and a signed attendance roster. The personnel designee posts the hours to each employee's in-service record. For online training, the employee files the completion certificate.

On November 1 each year, the personnel designee lists each aide and CNA who has not completed the required in-service hours and gives the list to the RN Supervisor, who schedules make-up sessions before December 31.
The Administrator reviews the training tracker quarterly and reports gaps to the governing body (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Plans and delivers orientation and in-service training, evaluates aide competency and signs the evaluations.
Makes sure that no one serves clients before orientation, and that CPR and in-service requirements are met.
Maintains the training tracker, CPR expiration dates and training records in personnel files.
Attend training, keep CPR current and give the agency copies of cards and certificates.

documentation: Signed orientation record with date, topics, hours and trainer
RN competency evaluation for each aide and CNA
Record of 2-hour medication-assistance training and the label-reading check
Current CPR card with expiration date
Annual in-service calendar, rosters, topics and hours for each employee
Training tracker and quarterly review

policies.title: Dementia-Related and HIV/AIDS Staff Training
policies.applies_to: Non-skilled Home Health Agency license and Homemaker and Companion Services registration: staff with client contact
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers receive the dementia-related and HIV/AIDS training Florida requires, within the required time frames, and that certificates are kept.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides dementia-related training under s. 430.5025, F.S.: basic information about dementia at hire, a 1-hour course within 30 days for staff with client contact, and 2 additional hours within 7 months for home health agency and companion/homemaker staff. Home health agency staff must complete the s. 430.5025 training (s. 400.4785, F.S.). Each employee completes the one-time HIV/AIDS course within 30 days of employment (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(r), F.A.C.). Certificates are kept in each personnel file. If [AGENCY NAME] claims that it provides special care for clients with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, it discloses the services that make it suitable for those clients, as required by s. 400.4785(2), F.S.

definitions.definition: The training required by s. 430.5025, F.S., from an approved provider: basic information at hire, a 1-hour course and 2 additional hours.
A one-time course completed within 30 days of employment, required by Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(r), F.A.C.
Any advertising or statement that the agency is suitable for, or provides specialized care to, clients with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders.

procedures: On the first day of employment, the personnel designee records the hire date and enters the 30-day and 7-month deadlines for each employee in the training tracker.

At hire, and before the first client visit, the trainer gives each employee basic information about dementia (what it is, common behaviors, how to communicate and how to report concerns). The trainer records the date on the orientation record (PER-04).

Within 30 days of hire, each employee with client contact completes the 1-hour dementia course from a provider approved to teach it. The employee gives the certificate to the personnel designee within 3 working days of completion.

Within 7 months of hire, each home health agency, homemaker or companion employee completes the 2 additional hours of dementia training required by s. 430.5025, F.S. The personnel designee files the certificate when received.

Within 30 days of hire, each employee completes the one-time HIV/AIDS course and gives the certificate to the personnel designee. The employee does not need to repeat the course unless agency policy changes.
The personnel designee reviews the tracker every week. The designee reminds employees and supervisors 10 days before each deadline.

If an employee has not finished the 1-hour course or the HIV/AIDS course by day 30, the RN Supervisor informs the Administrator. The Administrator documents the reason and arranges immediate completion. The Administrator decides whether the employee's client contact is limited until it is done.

If an employee has transferred in prior training, the personnel designee confirms that the certificate is from an approved provider and meets the hours, and files a copy. If the content or hours are unclear, the RN Supervisor reviews and decides whether additional training is required.

Before the agency uses any advertising, brochure or website language that describes services for people with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders, the Administrator reviews it. If the agency makes a special-care claim, the Administrator prepares a written disclosure describing the services and staff training that make the agency suitable, provides it to clients and prospective clients, and files it. If the agency makes no such claim, it does not use such language (see GOV-03).
The RN Supervisor uses the QA process (GOV-07) to identify caregivers who need additional dementia-care coaching, based on incidents, complaints or supervisory visits.
The Administrator checks the tracker monthly and records any missed deadlines and how they were resolved.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure all required training is completed on time and reviews any special-care advertising and disclosure.
Delivers basic dementia information at orientation and reviews outside certificates and coaching needs.
Maintains the tracker, reminds staff and files certificates.
Complete the courses by the deadlines and submit certificates.

documentation: Dementia training certificates (1-hour and 2-hour courses) in each personnel file
Record of basic dementia information given at hire
HIV/AIDS course certificate in each personnel file
Training tracker with hire date and deadlines
Written disclosure of Alzheimer's-related services, if a special-care claim is made
Records of late completion and corrective action

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: Non-skilled Home Health Agency license and Homemaker and Companion Services registration: all employees with client contact
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from communicable disease by screening employees for tuberculosis at hire and after exposure, keeping health records confidential, and excluding ill staff.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] screens employees for tuberculosis (TB) at hire and after known exposure, and sets any further screening schedule through the agency's infection-control policy (SAF-03), using current CDC guidance and OSHA requirements, in line with Rule 59A-8.0095, F.A.C. This manual does not state a TB test interval because the research for this manual did not retrieve a Florida rule prescribing one. The agency's written schedule is set by the RN Supervisor and approved by the Administrator. Screening results are recorded in the personnel file and kept apart from the general file. Staff with a communicable illness are excluded from client contact until cleared. Where OSHA requires, the agency offers hepatitis B vaccination and provides protective equipment, in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.1030 (bloodborne pathogens) and 29 CFR 1910.132 (personal protective equipment).

definitions.definition: A TB symptom review plus a test method (such as a skin test or blood test) chosen under the agency's infection-control policy and current CDC guidance.
Contact with a person who has confirmed or suspected active TB, or any other documented exposure to a communicable disease the agency has identified.
A confidential file of health information kept apart from the general personnel file, with access limited to the Administrator and the RN Supervisor.
Removal of an employee from client contact because of a communicable illness, until cleared.

procedures: The RN Supervisor writes the employee TB screening schedule into the infection-control plan (SAF-03), based on CDC guidance and the agency's risk assessment. The Administrator approves it, and the schedule is reviewed each year.
Before the first client visit, each new employee with client contact completes a health screening form and a TB screening under the approved schedule. The employee provides the result.

The personnel designee reviews the result for completeness (date, method, reading and signature of the provider). The RN Supervisor reviews any positive or unclear result and requires follow-up with the employee's health care provider before client contact.

An employee with a positive screening, symptoms of active TB or a known exposure is referred to a health care provider immediately. The employee has no client contact until the provider clears the employee in writing.

After a known exposure, the RN Supervisor arranges a screening and follow-up as directed by the employee's provider or the county health department. The Administrator documents the exposure, the follow-up and the date of clearance.
At hire and annually, the RN Supervisor reviews the agency's exposure risk and training with each employee. Training covers hand hygiene, standard precautions and protective equipment (SAF-03).

The personnel designee records screening dates, results and clearance in the medical file, kept apart from the general personnel file, in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic folder. Access is limited to the Administrator, the RN Supervisor and the personnel designee. Diagnoses are not shared with clients or coworkers.

Employees must tell the RN Supervisor before reporting for a shift if they have fever, productive cough, diarrhea, vomiting, an open or draining skin lesion or another communicable illness. The scheduler arranges replacement coverage so that no client visit is missed (SVC-09).
The RN Supervisor decides when an employee may return to client contact, using the employee's provider note when needed. The RN Supervisor records the decision and the date.

Where an employee has a reasonably anticipated exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material, the Administrator offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to the employee, as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires. The employee may decline in writing. The agency provides required protective equipment under 29 CFR 1910.132 and records distribution and training.

After any exposure incident (needlestick, blood or body-fluid contact), the employee reports it to the RN Supervisor immediately, receives medical evaluation as required by the OSHA standard, and the event is recorded under SAF-02 and SAF-04.
The Administrator reviews the screening tracker every quarter and reports any overdue screenings to the governing body (GOV-07).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the screening schedule, makes sure employees are screened and excluded as needed, and offers vaccination and protective equipment.
Sets the schedule from CDC and OSHA guidance, reviews results and decides return-to-work.
Collects results, keeps the medical file confidential and tracks due dates.
Complete screening, report symptoms and exposures, and stay out of client contact when ill.

documentation: Written employee TB screening schedule in the infection-control plan
TB screening result for each employee, with date, in the confidential medical file
Exposure follow-up and clearance records
Exclusion and return-to-work notes
Hepatitis B vaccination offer, acceptance or signed declination
Protective equipment and exposure-incident training records
Quarterly screening tracker review

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted staff of [AGENCY NAME]: administrator, alternate administrator, supervising RN, CNAs, home health aides, homemakers, companions and office staff. Applies to the non-skilled Home Health Agency license and to the Homemaker and Companion Services registration.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps a complete, current and retrievable personnel file for every staff member. The file must prove, before and during service, that the person is qualified, screened, trained and competent. A state surveyor must be able to check this at any time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps one personnel file for each employee and contracted caregiver. No caregiver is scheduled for client service until the file shows the required qualifications. For a home health aide or CNA, the file contains: (1) proof of current Florida CNA certification or a copy of another state's current certificate, OR documentation of 40 hours of aide training or a passed competency test (AHCA Form 3110-1007), as required by Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(b)-(c), F.A.C.; (2) the 2 hours of medication-assistance training, including the label-reading check, under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)15; (3) current CPR and annual in-service training for each calendar year under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(k); (4) HIV/AIDS training completed within 30 days under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(r); and (5) dementia-related training (see PER-05). Every personnel file, including those for homemakers, companions and office staff, also contains level 2 background screening results under s. 408.809, F.S., the documented employment-history verification attempts, the signed job description and the orientation record. Aide files also contain the RN competency evaluation. Training records for staff who serve APD iBudget clients are kept for at least 5 years, as required by the iBudget Handbook. [AGENCY NAME] applies the same 5-year standard to all personnel files after separation. Personnel files are confidential, are kept separately from client records, and are available to AHCA surveyors on request.

definitions.definition: The complete record, paper or electronic, of one staff member's qualifications, screening, training, competency and employment documents.

Two documented attempts to verify a person's employment or contractual history, as described in Rule 59A-8.025(7), F.A.C. Each attempt records the date, the method, the person contacted and the result.
Fingerprint-based background screening under s. 408.809, F.S., repeated at least every 5 years.
AHCA Form 3110-1007: all 14 practical tasks and at least 90 of 104 written questions passed. Skills must be demonstrated in person.

procedures: Before an offer of employment or contract is final, the Administrator (or designee) opens a personnel file using the [AGENCY NAME] Personnel File Checklist.
The Administrator obtains the applicant's application, résumé or work history, and government-issued identification, and places them in the file.

The Administrator submits fingerprints for level 2 screening through the Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse before the person has direct client contact (see PER-03). The screening result is filed. A caregiver is not scheduled until a cleared result is on file.

The Administrator makes and documents two attempts to verify each relevant employer or contract history (diligent effort). Each attempt is recorded on the Employment Verification Log with the date, method, contact and result. The log is kept in the file.

For a CNA, the Administrator verifies the Florida certificate on the Florida Board of Nursing / DOH license verification site and files a dated printout. A CNA certified in another state supplies a copy of the current certificate, which is filed.

For an aide who is not a CNA, the Administrator files either the certificate of 40 hours of aide training or the completed AHCA Form 3110-1007 showing a passing result. The Administrator confirms the record shows in-person skills demonstration, even if classroom content was online or hybrid (see PER-02).
The Administrator files the record of 2 hours of medication-assistance training, including the label-reading check, before the aide assists with any medication (see SVC-08).
The Administrator files the current CPR card and tracks its expiration date.
Within 30 days of hire, the Administrator files proof of the HIV/AIDS course (see PER-05). The dementia-related training record is filed as required by PER-05.
On the first day of employment, the employee signs and dates the job description and the orientation record. Both are filed (see PER-04).
The supervising RN completes and signs the competency evaluation before the aide's first unsupervised assignment (see PER-04). The RN gives the original to the Administrator for filing.

After each calendar-year in-service session, the trainer gives the Administrator a signed attendance and content record. The Administrator files it within 7 days and records the hours on the Training Tracker.

The Administrator reviews the Training Tracker monthly and flags any expiring CPR card, overdue in-service or approaching 5-year rescreening date. Staff with an expired requirement are removed from the schedule until it is corrected.
Employee health and TB screening records are kept in a separate, locked confidential section of the file (see PER-06).
For staff who serve APD iBudget clients, the Administrator keeps training records for at least 5 years and notes the retention date on the file index.

Files are stored in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system at [ADDRESS]. Electronic files are access-restricted, backed up and retrievable on demand during an unannounced survey (see GOV-09).

When an employee separates, the Administrator marks the separation date and retains the file for at least 5 years from that date. Files are then destroyed by shredding or secure deletion, and the destruction is logged.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the personnel file system, verifies every required item before scheduling, reviews the Training Tracker monthly, and produces files for surveyors.
Performs the Administrator's file duties and produces files for surveyors when the Administrator is unavailable.
Completes and signs competency evaluations, and gives training and competency documents to the Administrator for filing.
Provides accurate documents, signs the job description and orientation record, and gives the agency renewed CPR, certificate or other credentials before they expire.
File documents promptly, protect confidentiality and report missing or expiring items to the Administrator.

documentation: Personnel File Checklist for each employee
CNA certificate verification, other-state certificate copy, 40-hour training certificate or AHCA Form 3110-1007 result
Medication-assistance training and label-reading check record
CPR card, annual in-service records, HIV/AIDS and dementia training records
Level 2 screening results and Employment Verification Log (two attempts per history)
Signed job description, orientation record and RN competency evaluation
Training Tracker and file index showing retention dates
Record destruction log

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: All hourly and salaried employees of [AGENCY NAME], including home health aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions, the supervising RN and office staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee at least the Florida minimum wage, pays overtime as required, counts all working time (including travel between clients), and carries workers' compensation coverage.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee no less than the Florida minimum wage under Art. X, s. 24 of the Florida Constitution and s. 448.110, F.S. The minimum is $14.00 per hour from September 30, 2025 and $15.00 per hour from September 30, 2026. Local governments may not set a higher private-sector minimum wage (s. 218.077, F.S.), so the state rate controls in every county we serve. As a third-party employer, [AGENCY NAME] may not claim the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA, 29 U.S.C. 201 et seq.) companionship or live-in exemptions (29 CFR 552.109), so overtime is paid at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Time spent traveling between clients during the workday is paid working time. [AGENCY NAME] carries workers' compensation insurance. Coverage is mandatory for a non-construction employer with four or more employees, and part-time employees count toward that number (s. 440.02, F.S.). [AGENCY NAME] tracks each scheduled minimum-wage change and adjusts pay and client prices before the effective date.

definitions.definition: A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods) set by [AGENCY NAME] as [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME], used to calculate overtime.
All time an employee is required or allowed to work, including client visits, paid travel between clients, required training, orientation and staff meetings.
The hourly rate used to compute overtime, including most non-discretionary bonuses and differentials.
An agency that employs the caregiver and is paid to supply care to a client. Such an employer may not claim the FLSA companionship or live-in exemptions (29 CFR 552.109).

procedures: The Administrator classifies all caregivers as hourly, non-exempt employees. No caregiver is classified as exempt under the companionship or live-in exemptions.

Each year before September 30, and whenever the state announces a change, the Administrator checks the current Florida minimum wage. The Administrator records the rate, its effective date and the next scheduled change on the Wage Compliance Calendar.
At least 60 days before any scheduled increase, the Administrator compares every employee's hourly rate to the new minimum. Rates are raised where needed, effective on or before the effective date.

At the same time, the Administrator reviews client rates and payer rates (private-pay, SMMC LTC plan, APD iBudget, Area Agency on Aging). The Administrator documents any rate change needed to cover the higher wage and gives clients advance written notice under CR-07.
Caregivers record their time through the Electronic Visit Verification and timekeeping system (see SVC-10), clocking in and out at each client's home.

Time between the end of one client visit and the start of the next, when it falls within the same workday, is entered as paid travel time. Time to and from home before the first visit and after the last visit is treated according to the Administrator's written commute rule, [COMMUTE-TIME RULE].
Required orientation, in-service training, competency evaluations and staff meetings are recorded and paid as hours worked.
Employees may not work off the clock. Supervisors may not ask or allow unrecorded work. Employees report any unpaid time to the Administrator at once.

The Scheduler reviews hours at least twice each workweek. Before any caregiver reaches 40 scheduled hours, the Scheduler notifies the Administrator so overtime is approved in advance or the schedule is adjusted.
Payroll staff compute overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate for all hours over 40 in the workweek. This includes live-in or long-shift assignments, where all hours worked are counted.
Before each payroll is released, the Administrator or a designee compares EVV and timesheet hours to the payroll register. Differences are corrected and documented.

The Administrator counts all employees, full-time and part-time, every quarter. Workers' compensation coverage is kept in force at all times through [WORKERS' COMPENSATION CARRIER]. The certificate is kept at [ADDRESS] and renewed before expiration.
The Administrator posts or provides required wage notices, including the current Florida minimum wage notice, in a visible location and in the employee handbook.
Employees report any suspected pay error to the Administrator. The Administrator investigates within 5 business days, corrects any underpayment on the next payroll or sooner, and records the outcome.
Payroll records, timesheets, EVV data and rate-change documents are retained for at least 5 years.
The Administrator reviews this policy and the Wage Compliance Calendar each year at the annual policy review (see GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures minimum wage, overtime and travel-time pay compliance; tracks wage changes; maintains workers' compensation coverage; approves overtime.
Compute pay accurately from verified time records, apply the overtime rule and keep payroll records.
Monitors weekly hours, alerts the Administrator to potential overtime and schedules travel time realistically.
Records all time worked accurately, never works off the clock and reports pay errors.
Records time spent on supervisory visits and competency evaluations and does not ask for unrecorded work from caregivers.

documentation: Wage Compliance Calendar showing the current and next minimum wage and effective dates
Employee pay-rate records and rate-change notices
EVV and timesheet records, travel-time entries and payroll registers
Overtime approval records
Workers' compensation certificate and quarterly employee-count record
Pay-error investigation and correction records
Client rate-change notices (see CR-07)

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted staff of [AGENCY NAME], including aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions, the supervising RN, office staff and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To protect clients from exploitation, abuse, neglect and boundary violations by setting clear standards of conduct and by providing a safe way to report concerns.
policies.policy: Every staff member treats each client with respect and protects the client's privacy and property. Aide training covers respect for the client, privacy and property (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c), topic 8, F.A.C.), and [AGENCY NAME] applies that standard to all staff. Staff may not: accept gifts, tips or loans from clients or families; lend money to clients; conduct personal business with a client; use a client's property, vehicle, accounts or phone for personal use; disclose client information on social media or to anyone without authorization; or take photographs or video of clients for non-care purposes. Staff report any boundary concern to the Administrator promptly. Violations lead to discipline up to and including termination. Staff who suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation of a client must report it to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873, and the Administrator reviews the facts under SAF-01. Level 2 screening under s. 408.809, F.S., is a condition of employment, and a screening-disqualifying offense results in removal from direct client contact.

definitions.definition: The limit that separates a caregiver's professional role from personal, financial or social relationships with a client or the client's family.

Any conduct that crosses a professional boundary, such as accepting gifts, borrowing money, personal business dealings, sharing personal problems, romantic or sexual contact, or posting about a client online.
Improper use of a client's funds, property or assets for the benefit of someone other than the client.
The Florida Department of Children and Families hotline at 1-800-962-2873, which accepts reports of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of vulnerable adults.

procedures: At hire, the Administrator gives each staff member the Code of Conduct and Professional Boundaries. The staff member signs and dates an acknowledgment, which is filed in the personnel file (see PER-07).
During orientation, the supervising RN or trainer teaches respect for the client, privacy and property, and reviews examples of boundary violations (see PER-04).

Staff decline all gifts, tips, loans and bequests from clients and families. If a client insists, the staff member explains that agency policy does not allow it and reports the offer to the Administrator the same day (see CR-05).
Staff do not borrow, lend or hold money, credit cards, PINs or checks for clients. Any approved errand involving client funds follows the receipt and log procedure in CR-05.
Staff do not use client property, vehicles, phones, computers or food for personal purposes.
Staff do not engage in personal business, sales or fundraising with clients or their families. They do not accept private work from a client outside the agency's service agreement.
Staff do not post, text or discuss client names, photos, addresses, conditions or details on social media or with unauthorized people (see CR-04).
Staff do not give out personal phone numbers or social-media contacts to clients or family. They route scheduling and care questions through the agency office at [PHONE].

A staff member who has a boundary concern, receives an improper request or notices another employee crossing a boundary reports it to the Administrator immediately. If the concern involves the Administrator, the report goes to [GOVERNING BODY CONTACT].

If the concern may involve abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member (or the Administrator) calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately and follows SAF-01. Reporting to the Administrator does not replace the hotline report.
The Administrator documents each boundary concern on the Conduct Report Form on the day it is received, including date, people involved, facts and immediate protective action.

The Administrator investigates within 5 business days and, when needed, removes the staff member from the client's schedule during the review. The Administrator interviews the client, the staff member and witnesses.

If a violation is confirmed, the Administrator applies discipline proportional to the violation, up to and including termination. The Administrator records the outcome in the personnel file and, where required, reports under SAF-01, SAF-02 and REC-03.
Staff who report in good faith are protected from retaliation. Retaliation is itself a violation of this policy.
The Administrator reviews boundary complaints at each quality assurance meeting and uses patterns to adjust training (see GOV-07).
Each year, the Administrator repeats boundary training as part of annual in-service (see PER-04) and obtains a new signed acknowledgment.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, investigates reports, applies discipline and makes required hotline and state reports.
Teaches and reinforces boundaries, watches for boundary concerns during supervisory visits and reports them to the Administrator.
Follow the Code of Conduct, decline gifts, protect client privacy and property, and report concerns, including suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, at once.
Receives and acts on concerns involving the Administrator and reviews conduct trends.

documentation: Signed Code of Conduct and Professional Boundaries acknowledgment for each staff member
Orientation and annual in-service training records on respect, privacy and property
Conduct Report Forms, investigation notes and discipline records
Abuse Hotline report confirmation numbers and SAF-01 / SAF-02 reports
Gift-refusal and client-funds logs (see CR-05)

policies.title: Client Records, Electronic Signatures and Retention
policies.applies_to: All client records of [AGENCY NAME] under its non-skilled Home Health Agency license, including aide and CNA clients and the service provision plan for clients who have no treatment order.
policies.purpose: To make sure every client has a complete, accurate, confidential record that can be retrieved at any time, that is signed and authenticated correctly, and that is kept for the required period.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for every client that contains: the referral source, the assessment, an identification sheet, the plan, signed and dated service notes, supervisory visit notes and a termination summary (Rule 59A-8.022(5), F.A.C.). For aide, homemaker and companion clients with no treatment order, the signed and dated written agreement is the service provision plan, and the plan is kept for 1 year after termination (Rule 59A-8.020(2)-(3), F.A.C.). Client information is confidential. [AGENCY NAME] discloses it only with the written consent of the client or guardian, except as otherwise permitted by law (Rule 59A-8.022(2)). Records are retained as required by s. 400.491, F.S., and must be retrievable during unannounced surveys (Rule 59A-8.022(4)). On request, [AGENCY NAME] transfers a copy of the record to another agency (Rule 59A-8.022(3)). Electronic signatures must be authenticated and dated, with safeguards against unauthorized access and a process to reconstruct records (Rule 59A-8.022(6)). The retention period adopted by [AGENCY NAME] is the longer of the period set by s. 400.491, F.S., or [RETENTION PERIOD IN YEARS] years after termination of services. In no case is a service provision plan kept for less than 1 year after termination. The Administrator confirms the current s. 400.491 period at each annual policy review (see GOV-06). Records stored offsite or in the cloud are kept in the continental United States, its territories or Canada. Safeguards follow 45 CFR 164.530(c).

definitions.definition: The complete paper or electronic file for one client, containing the items required by Rule 59A-8.022(5), F.A.C.

For aide, homemaker and companion clients without a treatment order, the written agreement that describes services; it is signed and dated by an agency representative and the client or representative (Rule 59A-8.020(2)-(3)).
An electronic signature that is tied to one identified person, protected by access controls, and dated, so it can be shown who signed and when.
A tested backup and recovery method that restores lost or damaged records to their prior state.

procedures: At intake, the Intake Coordinator opens a record in [RECORD SYSTEM] and records the referral source and an identification sheet (name, address, phone, date of birth, emergency contact, representative or guardian, physician, payer).
The supervising RN files the assessment in the record before services begin (see SVC-03).

The agency representative and the client or representative sign and date the written agreement. A copy is given to the client, and the original is placed in the record (see CR-07). For clients without a treatment order, this agreement serves as the service provision plan (see SVC-04).

The Administrator checks every new record against the Record Contents Checklist within 5 business days of admission: referral source, assessment, identification sheet, plan, signed agreement and consent forms.

Caregivers complete a service note for each visit, including date, times, tasks performed, client condition and any concerns. They sign and date it the same day, and the note is filed in the record within [NUMBER] days.
The supervising RN documents each supervisory visit in a note that is signed and dated by the RN, and files it in the record (see SVC-06).

Unsigned or undated notes are returned to the author within 2 business days for correction. A late entry is labeled as a late entry with the actual date written. Staff do not erase or overwrite original entries.

Electronic signatures are allowed only on a system that gives each user a unique login. The system must authenticate the signer, stamp the date and time, lock the entry after signing, and keep an audit trail. Staff do not share credentials.
The Administrator limits record access by role, reviews the access list quarterly and removes access the same day an employee separates.

Electronic records are backed up daily to a secure location in the continental United States, its territories or Canada. The Administrator tests the restoration process at least once each year and documents the result so records can be reconstructed.
Paper records are kept in locked cabinets at [ADDRESS]. Records leaving the office are carried in a closed, secure container and returned the same day (see CR-04).

Staff release client information only with the signed written consent of the client or guardian, or as otherwise permitted by law. The Administrator logs each disclosure with the date, recipient and purpose.
When another agency requests a transfer, the Administrator confirms the written request, sends a copy of the record within [NUMBER] business days and logs the transfer. The agency keeps the original.
When services end, the supervising RN completes the termination summary within 7 days and files it with a copy of the written termination notice (see SVC-12).

The Administrator keeps closed records for the adopted retention period, marks each with its earliest destruction date, and organizes them so they can be retrieved within the survey timeframe in GOV-09.
At the annual policy review, the Administrator confirms the current retention period in s. 400.491, F.S. If it exceeds the adopted period, the policy is revised at once.

At the end of the retention period, the Administrator authorizes destruction by shredding or secure electronic deletion and records the destruction in the Record Destruction Log. Records are never destroyed while a survey, complaint, investigation or legal hold is open.

responsibilities.duty: Responsible for record completeness, access control, retention, release of information and survey readiness.
Completes and signs assessments, supervisory visit notes and termination summaries, and reviews records for completeness.
Opens the record, collects the identification sheet and signed agreement, and files documents.
Writes, signs and dates accurate service notes on the day of the visit.
Oversees safeguards under 45 CFR 164.530(c) and reviews disclosures (see CR-04).

documentation: Client record with the items required by Rule 59A-8.022(5), F.A.C.
Record Contents Checklist for each client
Signed written agreement / service provision plan
Signed consents for release of information and disclosure log
Electronic signature authentication and audit-trail reports
Backup and restoration test records
Record transfer log and Record Destruction Log
Annual confirmation of the retention period under s. 400.491, F.S.

policies.title: Homemaker and Companion Confidential Client Record
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME]'s Homemaker and Companion Services line (registration under Rule 59A-8.025, F.A.C.). The same format may be used for aide and CNA clients, with the RN additions in REC-01.
policies.purpose: To keep a confidential record for each homemaker and companion client that contains every item required by Rule 59A-8.025(8), F.A.C., so that staff can serve the client safely and a surveyor can verify the record.
policies.policy: This policy meets Rule 59A-8.025(8)(a)-(h), F.A.C. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a confidential record for each homemaker and companion client with: (a) the client's full legal name, address, phone number, age, and the disability if it is the basis for service; (b) the name and phone number of the emergency contact, next of kin or legal guardian, and the physician; (c) a copy of any contract or written service agreement; (d) the services provided, with the duration and frequency of visits; (e) dietary restrictions, if the provider prepares, orders or accompanies the client to meals; (f) food allergies; (g) activity limitations pertaining to service delivery; and (h) a copy of any written termination notice. Records are confidential and are shared only with staff who need them to serve the client, with the client's written consent, or as otherwise permitted by law. The same record format may be used for aide clients, with the RN additions in REC-01. Homemaker and companion staff provide no hands-on personal care (see SVC-02). If a client's needs change so that hands-on help is required, the client is referred for assessment under the licensed home health agency line or to another provider.

definitions.definition: The file required by Rule 59A-8.025(8), F.A.C., for each homemaker or companion client.
Non-hands-on services such as companionship, light housekeeping, meal preparation, errands and reminders. They do not include hands-on personal care (see SVC-02).
The person the agency calls first if the client has an emergency or the agency cannot reach the client.

procedures: At intake, the Intake Coordinator creates the confidential client record using the Homemaker/Companion Client Record form, which has labeled sections (a) through (h) matching Rule 59A-8.025(8).

Item (a): the Intake Coordinator records the client's full legal name, address, phone number and age. The disability is recorded only if it is the basis for service, and only to the extent needed to provide services.

Item (b): the Intake Coordinator records the name and phone number of the emergency contact, next of kin or legal guardian, and of the client's physician. The Coordinator confirms the numbers by phone during intake.
Item (c): the agency representative and the client or representative sign and date the written service agreement (see CR-07 and SVC-03). A copy goes to the client, and a copy is filed in the record.

Item (d): the Intake Coordinator records each service to be provided, along with the duration and frequency of visits, in the service plan section. The Coordinator updates the entry when the schedule changes, with the date of the change.

Item (e): if staff will prepare, order or accompany the client to meals, the Intake Coordinator records dietary restrictions in the diet section. If none apply, the section is marked "None applicable."

Item (f): the Intake Coordinator asks every client or representative about food allergies and records the answer, including "No known food allergies." Allergies are shown on the caregiver's assignment sheet.
Item (g): the Intake Coordinator records activity limitations that affect service delivery, such as limits on lifting, walking, stairs or driving.
Item (h): if services end, the Administrator gives the client written notice of the termination date and reason (see SVC-12) and files a copy of the notice in the record.

Staff update the record within 3 business days of any change in contact information, diet, allergies, limitations or services. Staff date and initial each update.

If a caregiver observes a change that suggests a need for hands-on care, the caregiver reports it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator contacts the client and responsible party about a referral or assessment under SVC-03.
Records are stored securely with access limited by role (see REC-01 and CR-04). Staff share client information only with a signed written consent or as otherwise permitted by law.

The Administrator audits at least 10 percent of homemaker and companion records each quarter, or at least 3 records if fewer, against the checklist. Findings go to the quality assurance meeting (see GOV-07).

policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] makes every required report to the state on time, with a named person responsible, a deadline and documentation for each.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes these reports and keeps proof of each. (1) Application and insurance changes are reported to AHCA within 21 calendar days (s. 408.810(3), F.S.). (2) Changes of administrator are reported to AHCA, with the change forms and level 2 screening of the new person (Rule 59A-8.0095(1)(b), F.A.C.). (3) A change of address, counties served, or the opening or closing of an office is filed on Form 3110-1011 with zoning and right-to-occupy evidence (Rule 59A-8.003(8), F.A.C.). (4) A change of ownership is reported under Rule 59A-8.003(4), and client records transfer to the new owner. (5) The renewal application reports the patient count and the status of the CEMP (approved or submitted), and includes the affidavit of compliance with s. 408.051(3), F.S. (s. 408.810(14)). Home health agency licenses renew every 2 years. (6) AHCA is given 30 days' notice before discontinuing operation, and clients are notified (s. 408.810(4)). (7) Changes in emergency coordinator phone numbers are reported to the county emergency management office and the county health department (Rule 59A-8.027(4), F.A.C.). Reports that concern clients, such as abuse, neglect, exploitation or incidents, follow SAF-01 and SAF-02.

procedures: The Administrator maintains a Reporting Calendar listing every report in this policy, its deadline and the person responsible. The calendar is reviewed at each monthly management meeting.

Application or insurance change: when information on the application or insurance changes, the Administrator notifies AHCA in writing within 21 calendar days of the change. The Administrator files the submission and confirmation in the licensure file.

Administrator change: the Administrator or owner notifies AHCA of the change. The owner submits the change forms and obtains level 2 screening for the new administrator under PER-03. The owner designates a written on-site alternate and files that designation (see GOV-02).

Change of address, counties served, or office opening or closing: before the change takes effect, the Administrator files Form 3110-1011 with zoning documentation and proof of legal right to occupy the premises. The Administrator does not start service in a new county or office until the filing is submitted.
Change of ownership: the owner follows the change-of-ownership process in GOV-10. The owner arranges for client records to transfer to the new owner.

Renewal: the Administrator begins the renewal application at least [NUMBER] days before the license expires. The application reports the current patient count and the CEMP approval or submission status. It includes the affidavit of compliance with s. 408.051(3), F.S., and the required fees, insurance proof and financial documents (see GOV-03).
Before renewal, the Administrator confirms that the CEMP has been reviewed in the past year and approved or submitted to the DOH-designated contact (see SAF-05).

Emergency coordinator phone changes: whenever the emergency coordinator or a listed emergency number changes, the Emergency Coordinator notifies the county emergency management office and county health department in writing within [NUMBER] days. The Emergency Coordinator files proof and updates the CEMP.
Planned closure: the owner gives AHCA at least 30 days' written notice before discontinuing operation, and notifies each client in writing in the same period (see SVC-12 and SAF-06).

Record custody on closure: the owner arranges for custody of client records and tells AHCA where they will be kept. If custody cannot be arranged, the owner publishes notice weekly for 4 consecutive weeks, as required by s. 408.810(4), F.S.
License return: on closure, the Administrator returns the original license to AHCA (Rule 59A-8.003(10), F.A.C.) and files proof of return.
For every report, the person responsible saves a copy of what was sent, proof of delivery (such as e-mail confirmation, portal receipt or certified-mail receipt) and the date in the licensure file.

If a deadline is at risk, the person responsible informs the Administrator at least 5 business days before it. The Administrator ensures the report is filed on time and records the reason for any delay.
The owner and Administrator review this policy and the Reporting Calendar at each annual policy review (see GOV-06) and after each licensure survey (see GOV-09).

required_items.text: Written policies and procedures governing 24-hour availability to licensed professional nursing staff by active patients receiving skilled care. They must describe an on-call system in which designated nursing staff can communicate directly with the patient. (Skilled agencies only.)

A home health agency that does not provide skilled services shall have written policies and procedures that address the availability of a registered nurse supervisor during hours of patient service. (This applies to a non-skilled personal care agency.)

If the agency operates a satellite office, it must: (a) ensure coverage of professional staff based on projected clients; (b) coordinate care and services by staff; (c) ensure supervision and service provision when staff are absent; (d) maintain communication and integration of services between main and satellite offices; (e) provide access to patient records at the satellite office; (f) monitor daily clinical and administrative activities, services, personnel and administrative issues; (g) ensure periodic onsite visits by the administrator; (h) make the satellite office's hours available to the public if they differ from the main office. (Conditional on having a satellite office.)

Written designation of an on-site alternate administrator for the administrator's absences. This person has responsibility and authority for daily operation during those absences and must meet ss. 400.462(1) and 400.476(1), F.S.
The director of nursing must maintain and adhere to agency procedure and patient care policy manuals. (Not required for an agency that does not provide skilled care; see (2)(i).)

The director of nursing, administrator or alternate administrator shall establish policies and procedures on biomedical waste for agencies providing nursing and physical therapy services. (Applies only if those services are provided.)
Policies and procedures consistent with recommended CDC and OSHA guidelines for safety, universal precautions and infection control procedures.
Set or adopt policies for, and keep records of, criteria for admission to service, case assignments and case management.
Establish and adopt policies and procedures for the delegation process of nursing tasks and activities as specified in Chapter 64B9-14, F.A.C.

A process to verify that skilled nursing and personal care services were provided. The director of nursing must be able to produce a certified report of home health services provided by a named direct-service or contracted staff person for a specified period. The report is due to a surveyor within two hours of the request, or within three hours if the period requested is longer than one year.

An ongoing quality assurance program with at least quarterly documented review of a sample of active and closed clinical records. It must assure that: 1. the agency accepts patients whose service needs it can meet; 2. case assignment and management are appropriate, adequate and consistent with the plan of care, and plans of care are individualized; 3. nursing and other services are coordinated, appropriate, adequate and consistent with plans of care; 4. all services and outcomes are completely and legibly documented, dated and signed in the clinical record; 5. the agency's policies and procedures are followed; 6. confidentiality of patient data is maintained; 7. QA findings are used to improve services.

RN assignment of personal care tasks to LPNs, CNAs and home health aides. The RN maintains full responsibility for those tasks and must ensure the aide or CNA is qualified for each assignment based on training and experience.

RN supervisory visits of unlicensed assistive personnel under s. 400.487(3), F.S., with written consent from the patient or the patient's guardian or legal representative for the RN to enter the home. The RN provides on-site supervision as needed, based on the severity of the patient's condition and the aide's or CNA's training and experience. Supervisory visits are documented in patient files.
Provision in agency policies and procedures for annual evaluation of the LPN's performance of duties by the registered nurse. (Applies if LPNs are used.)

Before a CNA works, documentation of current Florida CNA certification (or a current out-of-state certificate). Before a home health aide works, documentation of at least 40 hours of training or a passed competency test. Training subjects: 1. communication skills; 2. observation, reporting and documentation; 3. reading and recording temperature, pulse and respiration; 4. basic infection control; 5. basic body functions to be reported to the RN supervisor; 6. maintenance of a clean and safe environment; 7. recognition of emergencies and follow-up; 8. physical, emotional and developmental characteristics of populations served, including respect for the patient or client, privacy and property; 9. personal hygiene and grooming techniques; 10. safe transfer techniques and ambulation; 11. normal range of motion and positioning; 12. nutrition and fluid intake; 13. cultural differences in families; 14. food preparation and household chores; 15. assistance with self-administered medication (minimum 2 hours of training, including verification that the aide can read the prescription label); 16. other pertinent topics.

Home health aide training must be performed by or under the general supervision of an RN with at least two years of nursing experience, one of them in home health care. An agency may instead administer the Home Health Aide Competency Test (AHCA 3110-1007) and must keep documentation of the aide's passing result. The practical portion must be administered and evaluated by an RN, or by an LPN under RN supervision.
Home health aides and CNAs must receive in-service training each calendar year and maintain current CPR certification from an approved provider.

Home health aide and CNA responsibilities include: 1. personal care activities in a written assignment by a licensed health professional; 2. maintenance of a clean, safe and healthy environment; 3. other activities taught by a licensed professional for a specific patient, limited to the listed tasks (a–l); 4. keeping records of personal health care activities; 5. observing and reporting appearance and gross behavioral changes to the RN; 6. supervision of self-administered medication, limited to the four listed steps.

Self-administered medication assistance: an RN review and reconciliation of all prescribed and over-the-counter medications, to confirm the patient is medically stable with routine scheduled medications. A licensed health care professional must inform the patient or caregiver of the arrangement and obtain written consent under s. 400.488(2), F.S. Permitted aide actions are listed in (5)(o)1-4.

Responsibilities the home health aide and CNA may not perform (the list starts at 1. therapeutic services requiring licensure and runs through at least 10). The fetched page was cut off partway through this list, so retrieve the full text from the rule.

Each home health agency shall have written policies and procedures that delineate the agency's position with respect to state law and rules on advance directives. The policies shall not condition treatment or admission on whether the individual has executed or waived an advance directive. Conflicts between the agency's policies and a patient's advance directive are handled under Chapter 765, F.S.

The advance-directive policy must include giving each adult patient, before services begin, a copy of 'Health Care Advance Directives – The Patients' Right to Decide' (AHCA, rev. April 2006) or an equivalent written description of Florida law.
The advance-directive policy must include giving each adult patient, before services begin, written information about the agency's policies respecting advance directives.

The advance-directive policy must include the requirement that the patient's medical record document whether or not an advance directive has been executed. A copy of any executed directive goes in the record. If no copy is received, the agency documents that it requested one.
DNRO: cardiopulmonary resuscitation may be withheld or withdrawn only if a valid Do Not Resuscitate Order is present, executed under s. 401.45, F.S. (Department of Health form; rule 64J-2.018).

Acceptance of patients or clients: there must be a reasonable expectation that services can be provided safely in the patient's residence. This includes the ability to communicate with the patient (or the patient's designee) through a same-language staff person or interpreter, or through translation technology. The agency must assure the patient receives services as defined in the plan of care or written agreement, including all assigned visits.

At the start of services, a written agreement between the agency and the patient, client or legal representative, including the information in s. 400.487(1), F.S. It must be signed and dated by an agency representative and the patient, client or representative. A copy goes to the patient or client and the original goes in the file.

For homemaker/companion clients and for home health aide clients who do not need a practitioner's treatment order, the written agreement serves as the service provision plan under s. 400.491(2), F.S. It is kept for one year after services end.

Termination of services for patients or clients needing continuing care: develop a plan and make a referral to another agency or provider before termination. Give written notice of the termination date, the reason (s. 400.491, F.S.) and the plan for continued services. This does not apply to patients paying privately who default through non-payment. The agency should provide social work assistance to help determine eligibility for government-funded programs.

A written comprehensive emergency management plan, prepared and maintained under s. 400.492, F.S., following the criteria in the CEMP (AHCA Form 3110-1022, Rev. March 2013), which is used as the plan format. The plan describes how the agency establishes and maintains an effective response to emergencies and disasters.
The completed plan is forwarded electronically for approval to the contact designated by the Department of Health. The agency reviews the plan annually and makes substantive changes.

Changes in telephone numbers of staff coordinating emergency response (including after-hours numbers) must be reported to the county Emergency Management office and the county health department. A new owner reviews the plan after a change of ownership.

In an emergency, all staff designated for emergency measures must be informed of their duties. If telephone service is unavailable, the agency must have a communication contingency plan (for example cell phones, ham radio, public announcements, driving to the home, or contacting police or rescue services).

On admission, inform patients and caregivers of the county special needs registry (s. 252.355, F.S.). Document in the patient file whether the patient will evacuate or stay, whether the caregiver can take over services, and whether the agency must continue services. For ALF or adult family care home residents, find out the facility's evacuation plan and document it.

On imminent threat of an emergency, contact patients needing ongoing services (and the ALFs and adult family care homes served) to confirm each patient's plan. Before an emergency, establish procedures stating to what extent the agency will continue care during and after it. Ascertain which patients staying home need agency care, and designate staff to continue services.

If the agency ceases operation during an emergency, it must inform affected patients, notify the ALFs and adult family care homes served, and make arrangements for nursing personnel to continue essential services. It must report its status to the local emergency operations center. When unable to continue services to special needs patients, the record must document the efforts made to comply with the plan.

Collect registration information for special needs patients who need continuing care in a disaster and submit it to the county Emergency Management office. Educate registered patients that special needs shelters are an option of last resort and that services may not equal those received at home.

Maintain a current prioritized patient list with the information in s. 400.492(2), F.S., and furnish it to the county health department and Emergency Management office on request. The record of each special needs patient must include the s. 400.492(1) information. The agency must keep in the special needs patient's home a list of patient-specific medications, supplies and equipment (names, dose, frequency, route, time, allergies, physician, pharmacy).

Homemaker/companion registration: the application must state the specific geographic area to be served. Providers holding a registration as of July 1, 2015 may keep serving the counties listed on it if a plan for supervision of staff working outside the primary geographic service area is documented.

Confidential client record (homemaker/companion providers): (a) client's full legal name, address, phone, age, and disability if it is the basis for service; (b) name and phone of the emergency contact, next of kin or legal guardian, and physician; (c) copy of any contract or written service agreement; (d) services provided, with duration and frequency of visits; (e) dietary restrictions, if the provider prepares, orders or accompanies the client to meals; (f) food allergies; (g) activity limitations pertaining to service delivery; (h) copy of any written termination notice.

On accepting a client, there must be a reasonable expectation that the requested services can be provided adequately and safely in the residence. The provider must obtain all needed service-delivery information and supply employees or independent contractors capable of delivering the contracted services, including all visits.

official.notes: I did not find a single AHCA policy checklist or plan-of-operation form for Florida personal care. The required_items list is therefore built from the Chapter 59A-8, F.A.C. sections that require written policies, plans or procedures. Item numbering follows the rule text. Florida licenses the agency on AHCA Form 3110-1011 (HHA) or Form 3110-1003 (homemaker/companion), and AHCA surveys compliance. The survey tool is AHCA's ASPEN 'Home Health Agencies' regulation set, which I located but did not review. The CEMP (AHCA Form 3110-1022) is the mandated format for the emergency plan, and DOH reviews it. Items marked conditional apply only to skilled agencies, to agencies that provide nursing or PT services, or to agencies with satellite offices or LPNs. A non-skilled agency is not required to have a director of nursing under 59A-8.0095(2)(i). A reviewer would expect one organized policy manual, plus the CEMP, the aide training and competency documentation, a sample service agreement, and a sample client record. A non-skilled agency must show RN supervision arrangements and RN supervisory visits. Not reviewed or fetched (check before relying on this list): 59A-8.0215 (Plan of Care), 59A-8.0216 (RN delegation), 59A-8.0219 (medication administration), 59A-8.022 (clinical records), s. 400.487 and s. 400.491 F.S., s. 400.509 F.S., s. 400.4785/430.5025 F.S. dementia training, and the licensure application and addendum forms. The Cornell LII copies are unofficial, and the official text is on flrules.org (Florida Administrative Code).
